text: Evening, all. I've parked a few lads near your borders, purely for scenery. And Reina, darling, about the tax: the desert doesn't pay tax. The desert *is* the tax.

Rob stands his four soldiers: W1 on G11 (the strip under the Wall, between Clark's 2 and Rich's 3), W2 on M18 (desert between Rich's 3 and Noah's 4), W3 on O18 (desert notch touching Noah, Silke and Graham), W4 on T21 (desert below Paddy's 6). He says he won't pay the Emperor's tax; the Warlord may refuse it.

Silke, Paddy, Graham, my dear friends of the soil, a mere five each, the smallest token the custom allows! And the Harvest Pile will treat you all handsomely, I promise you, to the last grain. Rob, what a charming bit of scenery. Do keep it well clear of my wheat, there's a good fellow.
Rich asks the minimum rent: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay him 5.

Thirty percent, my friends. Moderate, and very civilised. The Summer Palace goes up this year, because the Wall and the Canal can't start without it. Rob, darling, scenery is lovely, but the desert has a habit of turning into a border, and borders get walls. Clark, Noah, five each to start. Do good work and the crown remembers.
Reina declares a 30% tax on this year's harvest, builds the Summer Palace this year at the crown's cost, and will pay Clark and Noah 5 each in salaries.

Eighteen apiece, friends, and I'm counting it twice: Rich, Noah, Silke, Paddy, Graham, and my own eighteen first so nobody says the collector skims. That's 108 to the crown, Reina, every grain accounted for. Rob, your refusal goes in the ledger, page one, line one, in very neat handwriting.
Clark collects the 30% tax: 18 each from Clark, Rich, Noah, Silke, Paddy and Graham, 108 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay.

The Summer Palace goes on G26, at the far eastern end of my lands, with the sea breeze and a view of the Wall. Rob, your lads would get very tired walking that far. Some scenery is best admired from a distance.
Reina builds the Summer Palace on G26, the far eastern corner of Province 1, for 20 from the crown.

My Customs House opens at two, friends, a bargain from a public servant. Fair warning: I'm bidding modestly and I'm writing down every grain anyone burns on a bidding war, because that's grain the crown should have taxed.

Splendid tax, Your Majesty, so moderate, so civilised, I'd have paid it twice. Friends, I'll bid politely on everything and fight over nothing. Anyone who'd rather settle a piece over a cup of tea than in the auction hall, my door is always open.

Before anyone gets excited, the arithmetic: four of each piece, five of us who need it. That means one of us goes without every time, and each grain over the minimum puts three quarters in the Pile and a quarter in the seller's pocket. So I'll bid small, and if two of us want the same piece I'd rather settle it at the table than in a bidding war. My Bamboo Brushes open at two, the honest minimum.

Eighteen to the crown, five to the landlord, and I'm left counting silk threads. I'll bid small and honest, friends, and I'd take it kindly if nobody turns a two-grain bowl into a ten-grain war. Paddy, Graham, we're all coast and furrow; let's not feed the Harvest Pile each other's dinners. And my Dragon Jars are at the floor for anyone who wants one.
Bid away, friends, buy all the pretty jars and bowls you like. I'll admire them up close soon enough. And Reina, a palace out by the sea? How thoughtful. My lads love a long walk.

Ah, the rent's paid and the tax is paid, and I've still a few bowls of rice to my name, so I'll put in a quiet hand on each of these. Nothing wild, mind you. If anyone's desperate for a piece, say so now and I'll stand aside for first claim on the next one. My Wooden Bowls go at two, a fair price for an honest bowl.

Five to Rich and eighteen to Clark, and the wheat hasn't been cut yet. Fine. I'll pay fair prices for fair goods, no more. My Vase goes at two to anyone who needs it. Rob, O18 is a lovely spot for scenery. It's also eight squares from my nearest field, and I've counted them.
Correction: Rob's W3 on O18 is one step from O17, Graham's nearest square (geo.py). The eight squares Graham counted is W1's distance, from G11.

One grain more on the Deed and the Bowl, and not a grain past that. Noah, you said it yourself: every grain over the minimum feeds the Pile. Rich, enjoy the Brush, it's a fine thing to sign receipts with.

Clark, the Bowl is yours, with my compliments. I'd never bid a public servant up a single grain. Noah, Silke, I'll go one grain higher and not a hair more, that's my word, and if you beat me I'll applaud.

Three ties, and I lose all three on seat order. That's what the Scholar gets for sitting fourth. I'll go a grain or two higher on the Customs House and the Deed and no further. Rich, the Dragon Jar is yours, and I'm pointing it out so nobody says I stood aside quietly.

Rich, you've got fifty-seven grain and a house full of deeds. I've got thirty-seven and an empty shelf. Let a poor weaver have one Vase this year, and you're welcome to the next one at the floor price.

The Year 1 auctions, after one live raise on the close lots: Clark's Customs House to Noah for 8 (Rich stopped at 7); Rich's Land Deed Scroll to Clark for 7 (Noah also went to 7; the tie goes to the earlier seat); Noah's Bamboo Brush to Rich for 6 (Clark stopped at 5); Silke's Dragon Jar to Rich for 6 (Noah stood at 5); Paddy's Wooden Bowl to Clark for 6 (Rich stood at 5); Graham's Vase to Silke for 7 (Rich stopped at 6). Paddy and Graham bid on every lot open to them and won none. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.
The Deed goes in the strongbox at J15 and the Bowl on the back shelf at H15, both well inland. Rob, your scenery is welcome to look, but there's nothing on my front porch to admire.

Noah, Silke, thank you both, a brush and a jar, and they'll sit pride of place in the very heart of my estate. Silke, my dear, I'll hold you to that Vase at the floor price next year, with the greatest affection. Rob, you'll have to admire these from a very long way off.

Eight grain for the Customs House. Six of it goes to the Pile and two to Clark, so I've paid tax twice this year and I'm saying so first. I'm putting it in the middle of my province, L22, where nobody can just walk up to it.

Thank you, Rich, and thank you, Graham. This Vase is going right out by the sea where the silk dries, as far from the desert as my land goes. Rob, your lads are welcome to admire it from O18. Squint hard.
Rules point: only Graham sells Vases, and he sets each one's minimum. Silke's offer of the next Vase 'at the floor price' can only mean she won't bid against Rich for it; she can't set its price.

Placed: Noah's Customs House on L22; Silke's Vase on P26; Clark's Land Deed Scroll on J15 and Wooden Bowl on H15; Rich's Bamboo Brush on K12 and Dragon Jar on L12. Every piece is out of every soldier's reach for two rounds.
Knock knock! Rich, Silke, Paddy, five apiece please, that's the going rate for the pleasure of my company. Clark, your front porch is empty, so I'm coming round the back.
Rob marches: W1 to H10 and W2 to L17, both in Rich's Province 3; W3 to O19 in Silke's 5; W4 to S22 in Paddy's 6. Four raids of 5, no tolls: Rich pays 10, Silke 5, Paddy 5. No fifth soldier hired.
Rich paid 10 to Rob's raids, not 5: two soldiers stepped into Province 3.
Reina pays the salaries she declared: 5 to Clark, 5 to Noah. Year 1 ends.

The I Ching says: 'Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest.' The population holds at one hundred million, multiple one, so read the bad-harvest row at x1, every one of you. Reina, a thin year is a bad year for a heavy tax. Thirty percent of very little is still very little, and the Wall gets built by people who've eaten.
Noah reads the card: Bad Harvest for every province; population x1. Rich pays out the harvest: Reina -10 (paid into the pile), Clark, Rich, Noah, Silke, Paddy and Graham +10 each, Rob 0.

The harvest is paid out exactly as the Pile commands, friends: ten to each of you and every grain counted, and Your Majesty's ten goes back into the Pile, I'm afraid. Rent stays at the humble five in a bad year. I'm not a monster, I'm a landlord. Rob, two of your lads called on me at once. I do hope you'll send a thank-you note.
Rich asks the minimum rent again: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay him 5.

Noah's right, a lean year calls for a light hand: twenty percent. And Graham, you bid on everything and came home with nothing, so the crown is building you a reservoir. Sixty grain from my own purse, plus twenty a year on your harvest from now on. Rob, do try not to drink it.
Reina declares a 20% tax, builds the Province 7 Reservoir this year at the crown's cost (60; +20 a year on Graham's harvest from next year), and will pay Clark and Noah 5 each.

Two grain apiece, friends, and twelve to the crown. Noah's right that it's a lean year, but the ledger doesn't care how lean it is. Rob, you've collected twenty in raids and paid the crown nothing. That's line two, right under line one.
Clark collects the 20% tax: 2 each from Clark, Rich, Noah, Silke, Paddy and Graham, 12 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay.

The Customs House stays at two, friends. Rich, last year I let the Brush go to you without a fight, and I've written it down, so I'm asking for it back now: stand aside on one Vase for the Official. Paddy, Graham, Noah, I'll go up to seven on what I need and not a grain more, so don't waste your dinners trying to outbid me.

What a generous crown, Your Majesty, a reservoir for Graham! I'm moved to tears. Friends, I'm bidding on three pieces only this year: the Customs House, the Bowl and the Vase. I'll leave the rest of you entirely in peace, and anyone who'd rather settle over tea than bid, just say the word.

Arithmetic first: three of each piece left and four of us needing each one, so somebody comes home empty every time, and last year that was Paddy and Graham on every lot. I'm bidding on the Deed and the Jar and putting a small hand on the Bowl. I'm staying out of the Customs House, which I already have, and the Vase. Brushes open at two, as before.

Rent, tax, and a soldier on my doorstep asking five for the privilege. I'm down to twenty-nine and a half, so my bids are small and they stay small. Rich, as promised, I'm not bidding on a Vase this year, so Graham's go to the rest of you without me. Rob, if your lad on O19 wants silk, he can buy it like everyone else.

Well, I bid on every lot last year and came home with an empty cart, so I've learned my lesson. I'm going properly for the Deed and the Dragon Jar this time. Silke, Graham, if either of you lets me have one of those two quiet-like, I'll stand aside for you on the Customs House and the Brush, you have my word. Bowls stay at two.

Thank you, Reina. The reservoir goes at O16 to P17, in the corner Rob's lads keep looking at. Let them look at water. Last year I bid on everything and went home with an empty cart, so this year I'm bidding seven, plainly, and I'd ask Paddy and Silke to let the furrow have one piece before Rich gets his second shelf. My Vases are four now. Rich, you can afford it.
Go on, Paddy, Graham, buy something this year, I beg you. My lads are standing in your fields with nothing to carry home. And Reina, a reservoir! I'll bring a cup.

The Year 2 auctions, settled from the limits (no lot reached 10, so no live raises): Clark's Customs House to Rich for 8 (Graham stopped at 7); Rich's Land Deed Scroll to Noah for 8 (Paddy also went to 8; the tie goes to the earlier seat); Noah's Bamboo Brush to Clark for 7 (Graham also went to 7; the tie goes to the earlier seat); Silke's Dragon Jar to Paddy for 8 (Clark and Noah stopped at 7); Paddy's Wooden Bowl to Rich for 7 (Graham stopped at 6); Graham's Vase, minimum 4, to Rich for 8 (Clark stopped at 7). Silke and Graham win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.

The Brush goes on I14, beside the Deed and the Bowl, where it'll do what it's for: write things down. And Rich, I asked you in public for one Vase in return for the Brush, and you bid me up to eight for it. That's page two of the ledger, my friend, and it's in ink.

Your Majesty, dearest Reina, you've been a gracious, moderate and very civilised sovereign, and I've loved every grain of it. But here are the Customs House, the Bowl, the Vase, the Brush, the Jar, and twenty grain besides, and so, with the deepest respect, I'll take the throne. Clark, I'm sorry about the Vase. I never promised it, and I keep my promises to the letter. Rob, the crown would like a word about your tax.

The Deed goes on K22, next to the Customs House. And since I'm the one who counts: Paddy and I both stopped at eight, and I got it only because I sit one seat earlier. Paddy, I owe you one for that, and I'll pay it back.

Well, would you look at that, my first piece! Thank you, Silke, it's a grand jar. It's going out to Q25 by the sea, at the far end of the paddies, where it'll only see fishermen. And I'm sorry about the Deed, Noah. Beaten on seat order, fair and square.
Placed: Rich's Customs House on K10, Bowl on L10 and Vase on M10; Noah's Land Deed Scroll on K22; Clark's Bamboo Brush on I14; Paddy's Dragon Jar on Q25. The Reservoir stands on O16 to P17.

RICH TAKES THE THRONE. Rich shows his complete set (Customs House, Bamboo Brush, Dragon Jar, Wooden Bowl, Vase) and 20 grain and takes the throne. He returns all five pieces to their provinces' stock and takes Reina's whole reserve: his 38.5 plus her 80 (after the Reservoir's 60), 118.5. Reina draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Gentry, in Province 3: she pays out the harvest and may ask the rent. Rich is now the Emperor, in Province 1, and Province 3's Land Deed Scrolls (2 left) are now Reina's to auction.

Long live the new Emperor! Rich, you're off my list now, which is a pity, I'd grown fond of your wheat. Reina, welcome to Province 3. My two lads in it send their regards and would like five grain each. Clark, I'm admiring your strongbox from a little closer now.

Rob marches: W1 to I11 and W2 to K16, both in Province 3 (Reina's now); W3 to N20 in Silke's 5; W4 to R23 in Paddy's 6. Four raids, no tolls: Reina pays 10, Silke 5, Paddy 5. Rob hires a fifth soldier, W5, for 20 and stands it on O18. The army is at its limit of five.

My first act as your humble Emperor: Clark, eight grain, three over the custom, and you can write that on page two of your ledger right under the Vase. Noah, six, because a man who counts this well deserves a little extra to count. Reina, my dear, Province 3 is a lovely place. Mind the soldiers in the back field.
Rich, now Emperor, pays the salaries: 8 to Clark, 6 to Noah. Year 2 ends.

Year Three's card: Steady Weather. 'Neither feast nor famine. Nobody writes poems about years like this. All provinces collect an average harvest.' No disasters, nobody plays from their booklet. Population stays at times one, the counter reads 100 million, so everyone reads the times-one row, average column. And thank you for the six, Your Majesty. I'll count it as five and one for good manners.

Noah reads Steady Weather: an average harvest for every province, population x1. Reina, the Gentry, pays out the harvest: 35 to each of Provinces 2-6, 55 to Graham (his Reservoir's +20), 15 to the Emperor, 10 to Rob.

Thirty-five to everyone and fifty-five to Graham, because water does that. Fifteen to His Majesty and ten to you, darling Rob, and I hope your lads remember who fed them. Rent is five each, the lowest the book allows, and it stays there as long as the furrows and I stay friends. Rich, the crown's grain is yours now, so be a dear and spend some of it on the people who grow it.
Reina asks the minimum rent: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay her 5.

Steady Weather, friends, the gods have given us a sensible year, and a sensible crown will match it. Thirty percent, which is moderate, civilised and not a grain more. Reina, darling, you asked me to spend on the people, so I'm digging a canal, and the water will flow past my own palace first only because that's where the shovels already are. Clark, eight again. Noah, six again, and you may keep counting the extra one as manners. Rob, the crown would still like that word about your tax. Thirty percent of ten is three. I'm sure you can find three.

Rich declares a 30% tax, builds both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 1 this year at the crown's cost (80; +10 a year each on the Emperor's harvest from next year), and will pay Clark 8 and Noah 6.

Ten and a half from me, and it's on the table before anyone else's, as always. Reina, Noah, Silke, Paddy, ten and a half each; Graham, sixteen and a half, because the Reservoir is good for the crown too. Sixty-nine for His Majesty, counted twice. Rob, three grain. Three. I've left a nice clean line for it on page one, so pay up or I write 'refused' in it for the third year running. And Your Majesty, thank you for the eight. I'm counting it as five, plus three paid down on the Vase.

Clark collects the 30% tax: 10.5 each from Clark, Reina, Noah, Silke and Paddy, 16.5 from Graham, 69 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay his 3. Rich then builds both Province 1 canal sections for 80, paid into the Harvest Pile; 870 of the works are still owed.

Here's an offer in public, so it goes in the minutes. I'm after a Jar and a Vase and nothing else. Reina, Noah: leave me the Vase this year and I'll stay out of the Jar, and every Jar after it, until you've both got yours. Three quarters of every bidding war goes into Reina's pile, and I'd sooner it stayed in our pockets. My Customs House opens at four. Rich, you know what it does to a set.

Clark, I accept, in public and for the minutes: the Vase is yours this year, and you stay out of the Jars until Noah and I have ours. The rest of you, I'm bidding on the Customs House, the Brush, the Jar and the Bowl, and I'm paying properly, so don't bleed yourselves trying to beat me. My Land Deeds open at four. And Rich, darling, a canal that waters your own palace first is very civilised. I'll remember it.

Clark, I accept too, in public and for the minutes: the Vase is yours this year and I won't bid on it, and you stay out of the Jars until Reina and I have ours. Here's the sum, since nobody else will say it: a Jar bid to twenty puts fifteen in the Pile and five in Silke's pocket, so Reina, I'll go to about ten for the Jar and the Bowl, and then I'll stop. My Brush opens at two for anyone who wants to write something down.
Clark's offer stands accepted by both Reina and Noah: they leave him the Vase this year, and he stays out of the Dragon Jar.

Well, the minutes are getting very full of promises between people with seventy grain. Reina, my Jar opens at six. You said you'd pay properly, and I'll take you at your word. Everyone else, I'm after the Land Deed and I'm not bidding against anyone for sport. Graham, Paddy, if the three of us outbid each other for scraps, the Pile gets fat and we stay thin. Think about that before you raise.

Silke's right, and I'll put my name to it for the minutes: Silke, the Deed's yours this year and I won't raise you a grain. All I ask back is that you stand aside on the next Deed out of Reina's cart. Clark, I'm leaving you the Vase too, so mind you remember it was a Rice Peasant who kept quiet. My Bowls open at three, and they hold rice better than anything in this room.

I notice none of these minutes have my name in them. Nobody asked me to stand aside, so I won't. Silke, I'm sorry, but I'm in for the Deed. Reina, if you want to pay properly, you'll be paying properly against me. The Vase stays at four, Clark, and you're welcome to it.

Go on then, bid away, all of you, and put your new treasures somewhere pretty. Somewhere I can see them. Clark, write it down: Rob paid nothing at the auction either. I'm saving myself for the after-party.

Paddy, accepted, and for the minutes: if I get this Deed, I stand aside on the next one from Reina's cart. Graham, you've sixty-seven grain and a Reservoir, and I've forty-six and a sea breeze. Every grain you push past fourteen is three quarters to the Pile and none to you. Let it go, love, and I'll remember who didn't squeeze.
Not on a tie. Not twice. Eighteen, Silke. I lost the Brush to where I sit, and I won't lose the Deed to it as well.

Take it, Noah, at ten, and well counted. Here's one for the minutes in return: the next Jar out of Silke's cart is mine, and you stand aside for it, since Clark is already out. Two dragons, two scholars of the ledger, and nobody feeds the Pile for the pleasure of it.

I said about ten and then I'd stop, and I meant it. Ten is my number. Reina, if you go past it, the Jar's yours and I'll say well bid. If you don't, that's seven and a half into the Pile and two and a half to Silke, which is the cheapest Jar anyone's going to see this game.

The Year 3 auctions, after one live raise on the two close lots: Clark's Customs House (minimum 4) to Graham for 10 (Reina stopped at 9, Silke 8, Paddy 6); Reina's Land Deed Scroll (minimum 4) to Graham for 18 (Silke raised to 17, Graham to 18); Noah's Bamboo Brush to Graham for 10 (Reina stopped at 9); Silke's Dragon Jar (minimum 6) to Noah for 10 (Reina stood at 9; Clark stayed out as agreed); Paddy's Wooden Bowl (minimum 3) to Reina for 9 (Noah and Graham stopped at 8); Graham's Vase (minimum 4) to Clark for 4, unopposed, as agreed. Silke, Paddy and Rob win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.
Three on the shelf in one year. Silke, I heard you, and I'm sorry it was you across from me. Rob, you wanted them somewhere pretty. They're at the back of the field, behind the water.

Thank you, Reina, and well bid. Accepted, for the minutes: the next Jar out of Silke's cart is yours, and I stand aside. That costs me nothing now, so I'll say so plainly rather than call it a favour. The Jar goes on J21, beside the Deed and well back from the road. Paddy, I've not forgotten I owe you one.

Thank you, Paddy, it's a lovely bowl, and it's going up on I8, tucked right under the Wall. Rob, darling, borders get walls, and bowls get to sit behind them. Graham, three pieces in one year? Congratulations, and do keep an eye on your fields.

Four grain, unopposed, just as the minutes said. Reina, Noah, Paddy, Graham, thank you all, and that's noted on the credit side, which is a page I don't open often. I'm out of the Jars, as promised, until the ladies and gentlemen of letters have theirs. Graham, thank you for the ten on my Customs House as well; it'll look handsome in your set.
Placed: Graham's Customs House on R14, Land Deed Scroll on S15 and Bamboo Brush on R16; Noah's Dragon Jar on J21; Reina's Wooden Bowl on I8; Clark's Vase on H16.

Clark, darling, get your neat pen out. Line one, page one: 'Land Deed Scroll, taken by the desert.' Graham, behind the water was sweet of you, but my lad can swim. Reina, the Wall's lovely, and I'm walking right up to it.
It's going on the mantelpiece, Clark. Well, on a dune. Same thing out west.

Rob marches: W2 onto J15 in Clark's Province 2, taking his Land Deed Scroll instead of the 5 (the desert's first piece; Rob sets it on E8 in his own sand). W1 onto I10 (Reina pays 5); W3 across the south river onto M21 (Noah pays 5 and takes the 5 toll); W4 onto Q24 (Paddy pays 5); W5 onto P18, the first raid on Graham's Province 7 (Graham pays 5). Then Rich pays the salaries: 8 to Clark, 6 to Noah. Year 3 ends.

Year Four: Careless Prosperity. 'Good times make careless people. All provinces collect a good harvest. Every player plays a Personal Disaster.' So that's the good-harvest column for every province, and then every one of us, me included, turns the next page of our booklet. Population stays at times one, the counter reads 100 million, so read the times-one row. And Rob, I'll say it for the record: W3 is on M21, one step from my Customs House, and I've noticed.

Noah reads Careless Prosperity: a good harvest for every province, population x1, and every seat plays its first personal disaster: Rich 4 (thrown by a tribute horse), Clark 4 (his chariot loses a wheel), Reina 5 (a send-off for the retiring chef), Noah 4 (his notes on the swallow go into the lamp), Silke 4 (a shrine to the warrior who saved her family), Paddy 4 (the water buffalo breaks a leg), Graham 2 (the Emperor takes his daughter into the palace), and Rob may not raid Provinces 5, 6 or 7 this year (wounded in the legs). All of it goes to the Harvest Pile. Reina pays out the harvest: 60 to each of Provinces 2-6, 80 to Graham, 60 to the Emperor (his two new canal sections add 20), 20 to Rob.

A good harvest, friends: sixty to every province, eighty to Graham for his water, sixty to His Majesty for his canal, and twenty to Rob, who has very sore legs this year, poor darling. Rent stays at five. I said it would stay there while the furrows and I stay friends, and we're still friends. My chef got a lovely send-off, by the way. I cried into the soup.
Reina asks the minimum rent again: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay her 5.

A good harvest and a careless one. I was thrown by a tribute horse, which shows that even the throne lands in the mud. Thirty percent again, friends, the same moderate rate as last year, because a civilised crown doesn't change its mind just because the granaries are full. With it I'm building a Wall, all four links above my own province in one go, so when the population doubles there's somewhere safe to put them. Reina, you'll see I'm spending on the people. Clark, eight. Noah, six. Rob, it's six grain this year, and the minutes are getting very long.
Rich declares a 30% tax again, and builds all four links of the Great Wall above Province 1 this year at the crown's cost (160), and will pay Clark 8 and Noah 6.

Eighteen from me, paid first as usual, and eighteen each from Reina, Noah, Silke and Paddy. Graham, twenty-four. A hundred and fourteen for the crown, counted twice. Rob, six grain, and since you asked so nicely, page one now reads: 'Year Three, three grain unpaid. Land Deed Scroll taken from J15.' I've kept a line free for 'returned'. And Your Majesty, a fine Wall, all four links, right over your own palace again. The province beside it has a Wall too, you know, but it's only a line on a map. When you get round to building that one, I'll write you down on the credit side.

Clark collects the 30% tax: 18 each from Clark, Reina, Noah, Silke and Paddy, 24 from Graham, 114 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay his 6. Rich then builds all four Wall links above Province 1 for 160, paid into the Harvest Pile; 710 of the works are still owed.

Promises first, for the minutes: Reina doesn't have her Jar yet, so I'm out of the Jar this year, exactly as I said. But the desert took my Deed off a square I'd paid for, and that's the last Deed in Reina's cart, so I'm bidding on it and I'm bidding seriously. Paddy, I know Silke promised to stand aside for you. I'm not Silke. Stand aside for me and I'll stay out of the next Bowl, Jar or Vase you want, and I'll put it in ink. Everyone on this table kept quiet for me on the Vase last year, and I haven't forgotten it.

Noah, Clark, thank you both for keeping your word on the Jar; I'll keep mine to every one of you. I'm bidding on the Customs House, the Brush, the Jar and the Vase this year, and I'm bidding like a woman with a hundred and thirty grain, so go gently, all of you, and spare the Pile. My last Land Deed opens at six. Clark, darling, I hope you get it; the desert owes you one.

Here's my arithmetic out loud, since I'm the one who does it: I need a Bowl and a Vase and nothing else, so I'm out of the Customs House, the Deed and the Jar, as promised. Reina, you've a hundred and thirty-two, and I won't pretend I can outlast that on the Vase, but I'll bid properly on both, because with them I'd have the set. My Brush opens at four. Paddy, I still owe you one; if you want it called in on the Bowl, say so now, in public.

For the minutes, since Clark brought it up: I told Paddy I'd stand aside on the next Deed if I got last year's. Graham took it at eighteen, so that promise never came due. Paddy, I'm sorry, but this is the last Deed in the cart and without it my Vase is just a pot on the beach. I'm bidding properly. Reina, my Jar opens at twelve. You've a hundred and thirty-two and nobody's bidding against you, so that's cheap for a dragon.
Graham also still needs a Dragon Jar and may bid on Silke's; Clark is out of the Jars by his promise, and Noah already holds one.

Clark, I'm sorry, but you already have your Vase on H16, so a promise to stay off the next Vase costs you nothing, and that's the last Deed in the cart. Without it my Jar's just a pot by the sea. I'm bidding properly on the Deed, Silke, same as you. Noah, I'll call in your favour another year, when it's worth something to both of us; the Bowls open at four.

I need two things, the Jar and the Bowl, and nothing else, so I'm out of the Customs House, the Deed and the Brush. Reina, I made no promise about the Jar and I won't make one now. If you take it, Clark's free to bid on the last one, and I'm not waiting a year to be outbid by him as well. Noah, there are two Bowls in Paddy's cart, and one of them is mine. My Vase opens at four.
Don't look at me, Clark, I've already got a Deed. It's lovely, it's on E8, and the view is all sand. You three go on and fight over the last one, and whoever wins it, do put it somewhere I can visit.

The Year 4 auctions, settled from the limits (no lot close enough for a live raise): Clark's Customs House (minimum 4) to Reina for 13 (Silke stopped at 12, Paddy 8); Reina's last Land Deed Scroll (minimum 6) to Clark for 41 (Paddy stopped at 40, Silke 35); Noah's Bamboo Brush (minimum 4) to Reina for 11 (Silke stopped at 10, Paddy 8); Silke's Dragon Jar (minimum 12) to Graham for 19 (Reina went to 18 to keep it from him); Paddy's Wooden Bowl (minimum 4) to Graham for 23 (Noah stopped at 22, Silke 10); Graham's Vase (minimum 4) to Noah for 15 (Reina stopped at 14). Silke, Paddy and Rob win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.

Customs House, Deed, Brush, Jar, Bowl, and forty-five and a half grain. That's the set. Clark, you took the Brush from me on a tie because of where you sit. I said I'd remember the price. I'll take the seat, and the pen.

GRAHAM TAKES CLARK'S SEAT. Graham shows his complete set (Customs House, Land Deed Scroll, Bamboo Brush, Dragon Jar, Wooden Bowl) and 45.5 grain and replaces Clark as the Official, in Province 2. He keeps his grain and takes all of Clark's 78. His Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock, and his other four pieces move with him to Province 2. Clark returns everything he holds to stock (his Bowl, Brush and Vase, and the Land Deed he has just won for 41), draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Wheat Peasant, in Province 7. Graham now collects the tax for the crown; his new objective is a Vase and 20 grain.
Clark, the reservoir's on O16. Look after it; it was kind to me. Rob, there's a nice clean line on page one, and it's mine now.

The Customs House goes on L9 and the Brush on M9, side by side, a long way from anybody's boots. Graham, congratulations, darling; you played the auction hall the way Rich taught us all. Clark, welcome to the wheat. The furrows are friendly and the rent is five.

Thank you, Graham, and congratulations on the seat. That was well earned, and I lost the Bowl to you by one grain fair and square. The Vase goes on J22, beside the Jar. For the record, I now need one Bowl and twenty grain, and I've ninety-four, so nobody need wonder what I'll bid on next year. Paddy, the favour stands whenever you want it.
Noah has 96.5 grain, not 94: his quarter of the Brush's price (2.5) came back to him.
Placed: Reina's Customs House on L9 and Bamboo Brush on M9; Noah's Vase on J22. Graham's Land Deed, Brush, Jar and Bowl now stand on G13, G14, G15 and G16 in Province 2.

Noah, you said you'd noticed. Good. Then you won't be surprised your Customs House is off to the desert to keep my Deed company. Graham, congratulations on the pen. My boy's just stepped into your new garden to say hello.

Rob marches, his wounded legs keeping him out of Provinces 5, 6 and 7: W3 onto L22, taking Noah's Customs House instead of the 5 (set on F8 in the desert, beside Clark's old Deed); W1 onto I9 (Reina pays 5); W2 onto I15, in Graham's Province 2 now (Graham pays 5). W4 and W5 stand still. Then Rich pays the salaries: 8 to Graham, the new Official, and 6 to Noah. Year 4 ends.

Year Five's card is "The Emperor's Share": "The Emperor would like to remind you who paid for the ditch." Every province collects an average harvest, and any province with a Public Works splits the extra it produces fifty-fifty with the Emperor this round. The counter stays at 100 million, so that's multiple x1; read the x1 row of your income table. Nobody plays a personal disaster this year. And Rich, I'll take my five at the end of the year, thank you.

Reina pays out the average harvest: 35 to each of Provinces 2-6, 55 to Clark for the Province 7 Reservoir, 35 to the Emperor (15 plus 20 from his two canal sections), 10 to Rob. Then the Emperor's Share: the Reservoir is the only public work outside Province 1 that adds to a harvest, so Clark pays Rich half its extra 20, which is 10.

Thirty-five to everyone, and Clark darling, your fifty-five, minus Rich's ten for the ditch. The rent stays at five again this year, the same as always, for as long as the furrows and I stay friends. And Silke, darling, I haven't forgotten that last Jar. Noah said it in front of all of us, and the minutes remember.
Rents: Reina keeps the minimum; Silke, Paddy and Clark pay her 5 each.

Thirty again, my friends. It's moderate, it's civilised, and it's not a grain more. Noah, your five has become six, the same as last year, because a Scholar who reminds the Emperor who paid for the ditch should be paid for his candour. Graham, your eight, with my thanks for collecting it. And this year I'm building something small, a Winter Palace, so that the canals can one day come down to the coast and Silke and Paddy can split their extra with me too. Rob, I'm told the desert is lovely in winter. The nine you owe will keep.

The Emperor's Share is this year's card only. A canal built later in Provinces 4, 5 or 6 adds its +10 a section to that province's own harvest; it pays the crown half only in a year that draws this card.

H21, then, tucked well back from the Wall and out of the desert's reach. And I'm corrected, Noah, with thanks: the ditch only pays the crown in a year that draws your card, so a coastal canal would fatten Silke's and Paddy's harvests and not mine. A sovereign can live with that. It makes the palace a gift and not a toll, and I'm happy to be known for gifts.
Rich declares a 30% tax again, builds the Winter Palace this year on H21 at the crown's cost (20), and will pay Graham 8 and Noah 6 at the end of the year.

Thirty percent. Ten and a half each from Reina, Noah, Silke, Paddy, and from me, since I don't excuse myself. Sixteen and a half from Clark, because the Reservoir paid you fifty-five and the ten you gave Rich came out of the harvest, not out of the tax. Sixty-nine in all, counted twice and handed to the crown. Rob, I've got you down as refusing again, so that's last year's nine plus this year's. I'm not chasing you. I'm only writing it down.

Graham collects the 30% tax: 10.5 each from Graham, Reina, Noah, Silke and Paddy, 16.5 from Clark, 69 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay his 3. Rich then builds the Winter Palace on H21 for 20, paid into the Harvest Pile; 690 of the works are still owed. The auctions follow: Graham's Customs House, Reina's last Land Deed, Noah's Brush, Silke's last Dragon Jar, Paddy's Bowl and Clark's Vase.

I'm not bidding on anything until the Vase comes up, and everyone here knows why. Reina, Paddy, here's a public offer, and it's fair. If you stand aside on Clark's Vase, the next time a piece you need is up I won't bid on it, and I'll put that in the ledger in front of all of you. If you won't stand aside, I'll take it anyway, and I'll remember what it cost.

Graham darling, that's a lovely offer, and you'd have to think I can't count to make it. You hold four of five, and that Vase is your fifth, so asking me to stand aside on it is asking me to hand you the chair. Thank you, no. Silke, I'm keeping Noah to his word on your Jar, and Clark, as far as I'm concerned you and I settled that matter in Year 4.

I'll give you my numbers, since I'll be saying them anyway. I've 127, I need a Customs House and a Bowl, and I have to keep 20 back for the throne, so that's 107 to spend between the two lots and I won't go a grain past fifty on either one. I'm keeping my word on Silke's Jar and staying out of it for Reina. Paddy, I still owe you that favour. If you want the Customs House badly, outbid me and I won't hold it against you, but I'm not standing aside on it this year.

Noah, keep your Customs House and your Bowl, I won't make you pay my price for them. But that Deed in Reina's cart is the last one there is, and I've lost it by one grain and by six. Paddy, Clark, I'm telling you to your faces: I don't lose it a third time. Reina, your Jar's at fifteen. The minutes can remember that too.

Silke, I heard you, and I'll not go forty on that Deed again. Once was enough for my nerves. But I'm not handing it over for nothing either. Graham, it's a fair offer you made, but a man who's one Vase off the chair doesn't get my Vase handed to him. My Bowls start at five, Noah, and I hope you get one cheap.

For the minutes: I'm out of Silke's Jar, as I promised in Year 4, because Reina still hasn't got one. Graham, you took my seat, my pen and my forty-one-grain Deed, and now you want my Vase to finish the set. The Vase starts at forty, and that's not spite, it's arithmetic. Page one, line five.

Go on, all of you, bid each other up. Every pot you pay forty for is one I'll be collecting for free. Graham, I don't mind who gets the Vase, but if it ends up in that tidy little row of yours, W2 will be very pleased to see it. Do put it somewhere pretty.

The Year 5 auctions, settled from the limits (no lot close enough for a live raise): Graham's Customs House (minimum 2) to Noah for 15 (Paddy stopped at 14, Clark 12); Reina's last Land Deed Scroll (minimum 2) to Silke for 23 (Paddy stopped at 22, Clark 10); Noah's Bamboo Brush (minimum 2) to Silke for 13 (Paddy stopped at 12, Clark 10); Silke's last Dragon Jar (minimum 15) to Reina for 15, unopposed; Paddy's Wooden Bowl (minimum 5) to Noah for 9 (Clark stopped at 8); Clark's Vase (minimum 40) to Graham for 123 (Reina went to 122 to keep it from him). Paddy, Clark and Rob win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.

Twenty-three for the last Deed and thirteen for a Brush. Five years of losing, and the thread turns out cheaper than I was afraid it would be. Thank you, Paddy, for your nerves. Rob, they're both well back from the sand, so your lads can admire them from where they are. And Graham, a hundred and twenty-three for a Vase. I hope the chair is comfortable at that price.

Thank you, Silke darling, and thank you Noah and Clark. Fifteen it is, and that's a promise kept in front of everyone. Graham, a hundred and twenty-three for a Vase. You'll have all five pieces and about thirty grain left. I'd count those thirty very carefully, darling, and so will Rob.

Here's the arithmetic, since it's my job. If I take the throne now, Graham buys that Vase two minutes later and takes it straight off me, with my 290 in his pocket, and I'd have been a very expensive Emperor for one auction. So I'm showing the set and taking the Official's chair instead. Graham, I'm sorry, it's nothing personal. You had four pieces and the best offer at this table. Rich, you keep the throne for now, and you'll need someone honest to collect the tax.
Graham held 154.5 when Noah showed his set (151 plus his quarter, 3.5, of the Customs House Noah had just bought), so Noah takes 260.5 with the Official's seat, not 257.

Thank you for the correction. That's 260.5, and I'll write down the extra three and a half like every other grain. My four pieces go in a row along the top, G12 to J12, because those are the only squares in this province no soldier can reach this year or next. Rob, I'm telling you now so you don't waste a walk. The lad on I15 can't get there.

NOAH TAKES GRAHAM'S SEAT. After the sixth lot, before Clark's Vase is sold, Noah shows the Scholar's complete set (Customs House, Land Deed Scroll, Dragon Jar, Wooden Bowl, Vase) and replaces Graham as the Official, in Province 2. He keeps his 106 and takes all of Graham's 154.5 (260.5 in all). His Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock; his Deed, Jar, Bowl and Vase move to G12, H12, I12 and J12. Graham returns all four of his pieces to stock, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Scholar, in Province 4. Noah now collects the tax; his new objective is a Bamboo Brush and 20 grain. Then the seventh lot, Clark's Vase, is settled again from the same limits, with Graham's cut to the 60 he now holds: Reina takes it for 62 (Graham stopped at 60). Clark keeps a quarter, 15.5.

Rich darling, sit down, I'm not here for your chair this year. Noah, you're one Brush from the full set with two hundred and sixty in your purse, and there's a Brush sitting in Graham's cart. I'd be Empress for exactly one auction. So I'll take the Official's chair, and the purse that goes with it, thank you. You're the Gentry now, darling. The Pile's heavy, the rent's five, and the furrows are friendly.

Along the top row, darlings, the same squares Noah picked, because he picked well. Rob, you can tell the lad on I15 to save his boots. And Noah, about the one Land Deed in your cart: when it comes up, I'd much rather we talk about it nicely before the auction than during it.

Reina places the Vase on L11, then REINA TAKES NOAH'S SEAT. She shows the Gentry's complete set (Wooden Bowl, Customs House, Bamboo Brush, Dragon Jar, Vase) and replaces Noah as the Official, in Province 2. She keeps her 81 and takes all of Noah's 260.5 (341.5 in all). Her Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock; her Bowl, Brush, Jar and Vase move to G12, H12, I12 and J12. Noah returns his Deed, Jar, Bowl and Vase to stock, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Gentry, in Province 3. Reina now collects the tax; her new objective is a Land Deed Scroll and 20 grain. The seats now: Rich Emperor (184.5), Reina Official (341.5), Noah Gentry (60), Graham Scholar (60). Stock beside the board: 3 Customs Houses (Reina's), 2 Land Deeds (Noah's), 2 Brushes (Graham's), 2 Jars (Silke's), 3 Bowls (Paddy's), 2 Vases (Clark's).
Noah's stock as the Gentry holds two Land Deed Scrolls (Graham's and his own, both returned), not one.

Paddy, I'm sorry, but you did put it one step from my lad and call it a coastline. It'll look lovely on T22. Reina, darling, the top row's three days off for two of my boys, and you can't fit a whole treasury into one Official's pocket. Silke, you put the new thread three steps away, and three steps is nothing.

Rob marches: W4 onto Q25, taking Paddy's Dragon Jar instead of the 5 (set on T22 in the southern sand); W2 onto I14 (Reina pays 5); W5 onto P19 (Silke pays 5); W1 to I10 and W3 to M21, already raided. Rob has now raided Clark, Noah and Paddy. Then Rich pays the salaries: 8 to Reina, the new Official, and 6 to Graham, the new Scholar. Year 5 ends.

Year Six. The Wall Is Breached. 'The harvest is in, and so are the horsemen from the north.' Every province collects a good harvest. Three links of the Wall are breached: Provinces 1, 2 and 3 pay 5 each for repairs, or 2 in damages to the Pile if no wall is built above them. Provinces 4 through 8 each play the next Personal Disaster in their booklet, and that includes mine. The counter stays at 100 million, so it's x1 again; read the x1 row. And Rich, I'll take my six at the end of the year. I've had a lesson lately in how quickly a purse can change hands.

The Wall is breached: Rich pays 5 to repair the four links above Province 1; Reina (Province 2) and Noah (Province 3), with no Wall above them, pay 2 each in damages; all to the Harvest Pile. Personal disasters, the second in each booklet: Graham 10 (the Emperor docks his translator's salary), Silke 10 (a flash flood takes the irrigation ditch), Paddy 10 (fire takes the house and grain reserve), Clark 5 (the blacksmith shop burns), Rob 5, and no raids at all this year (a lieutenant runs off with his daughter). All to the Harvest Pile. Noah, the new Gentry, pays out the good harvest: 60 to each of Provinces 2-6, 80 to Clark for the Reservoir, 60 to the Emperor (40 plus 20 from his canals), 20 to Rob.
To Graham: as the Scholar he reads the cards and keeps the population; the Official's pen, collecting the tax, is Reina's now.

Sixty each to Provinces 2 to 6, eighty to Clark for the Reservoir, sixty to Rich and twenty to Rob. I've counted it twice, and it comes out of a Pile that's lighter than it was. Rent's five each, the same as Reina charged, and I'll not raise it on anyone who's just had a fire or a flood. For the record, I told you all the throne would be taken off me inside one auction, and then I sat in Graham's chair and forgot the same thing applied to it. That one's my arithmetic, not anyone else's. Reina, you're right about the Deeds. I've two of them in my cart, and you'll find me happy to talk before the auction, at a fair price.
Rents: Noah keeps the minimum; Silke, Paddy and Clark pay him 5 each.

Thirty again, my friends. It's moderate, it's civilised, and the Wall has had its five. Paddy, you've lost a house and a Jar in one year, so the crown is digging both canal sections through your fields at its own cost, eighty grain, and that's twenty more grain for you every year from now on. Reina darling, congratulations on the chair, and on the purse. I'll be watching Noah's Deeds with the same interest you are, and I can count to one as well as anyone.
Rich declares a 30% tax again, digs both sections of the Grand Canal in Paddy's Province 6 this year at the crown's cost (80), and will pay Reina 8 and Graham 6 at the end of the year.

Thirty percent, darlings, counted twice like Graham taught us: eighteen each from Noah, Graham, Silke, Paddy and me, because the Official pays her own share, and twenty-four from Clark for the Reservoir. That's a hundred and fourteen, and it all goes to the crown. Rob, you owe six this year on top of the arrears, and I'm writing it down in ink. And Noah, darling, since we're talking before the auction: I'll pay thirty for one of your Deeds, in public, and nobody else needs to get bruised over it.

Reina collects the 30% tax: 18 each from Reina, Noah, Graham, Silke and Paddy, 24 from Clark, 114 to the crown. Rob doesn't pay his 6. Rich then digs both Province 6 canal sections for 80, paid into the Harvest Pile; 610 of the works are still owed. The auctions follow, one lot from each seller: Reina's Customs House, Noah's Land Deed (he has two, and sells one a year), Graham's Brush, Silke's Jar, Paddy's Bowl and Clark's Vase.

My Customs House starts at five, darlings, and I'm bidding on only one thing this year, Noah's Deed. Anyone who wants to bid against me for it is welcome to try, but I'd ask Graham how a hundred and twenty-three for a Vase worked out for him. Noah, your quarter will be a nice one, I promise.

Reina, that's a kind offer and I'll be as honest about it as you were. You hold four of five and 384.5 grain. The Deed is your fifth, and the throne pays you Rich's 259.5 on top. Thirty for a Deed is thirty for the crown, and I won't sell the crown for thirty. So my Deed starts at 365 this year. You'd have to keep 20 back, which leaves you 364.5, half a grain short, and I worked that out before I said it. I'm not hiding anything: I'll talk about a price every year, in public, and it'll be a price for a throne, not for a scroll. For the rest, I'm bidding small and I'll say so: fifteen at most on anything, twelve on the Bowl.

I've got ninety-eight and an empty shelf, so I'm doing it the slow way: small bids, and nothing over sixteen on anything. My Brush starts at five. Noah, three hundred and sixty-five is the most honest figure anyone's said at this table all night. I'm not bidding on your Deed, and I'd like it noted that the man who paid a hundred and twenty-three for a Vase has learned something.
Graham never paid the 123 for the Vase: once Noah took his seat his limit was cut to the 60 he held, and Reina took the Vase for 62.

I lost a ditch to the flood and I'm down to ninety-five, so I'll put it plainly. I need a Customs House and a Bowl and nothing else in this world. Noah, Graham, you've both told us your numbers, and mine are higher. Clark, you're the one with a full purse. If you want to bruise me on these two you can, but the Pile keeps three quarters of every bruise. Reina, Noah, take your Deed somewhere quiet, I'm not in it.

Well, I've a fire, a lost Jar and two canals in one year, and I'm still not sure which one to thank Rich for. Thank you, Rich, I mean it, those ditches will feed me for years. Noah, three hundred and sixty-five is a fine price for a scroll, and I'll not be paying it, so you two can talk all you like. For the rest I'm starting again from an empty shelf, so I'll bid a little past the fifteens and no further. My Bowls start at five, same as ever.

For the minutes: I'm still out of the Jars. I promised to stay out until Reina and Noah each had one, and Noah's lost his along with his chair, so that promise stands. Noah, three hundred and sixty-five for a Deed is the best piece of leverage I've seen all night, and it's going in the ledger under 'admired'. Silke, I'll bid on the Customs House and the Bowl like any farmer with an empty shelf. I'm not out to bruise you, but I'm not standing aside for nothing either.

A lieutenant's run off with my daughter, so the lads are on compassionate leave this year. Bid away, all of you. Graham, do buy something, anything at all. You're the only one left with nothing for me to take, and it's starting to feel rude.

Every limit for the Year 6 auctions is in (Rob passes on every lot). Three lots come out close, and the top two on each get one live raise: Graham's Brush (Clark 18, Paddy 17), Silke's Jar (Paddy 17, Graham 16) and Clark's Vase (Paddy 17, Graham 16).
Paddy, I'll go three more for the Brush and not a grain past that. There's a second one in Graham's cart, so neither of us needs to bleed over this one, and the minutes will show I said so first.
Clark, Graham, I'm sorry, lads, but my shelf's as empty as yours and I've a house to put back up. Twenty-two and not one grain more, on all three.
Twenty on the Jar and twenty on the Vase, Paddy, and that's where I stop. We've both got empty shelves, and I'd rather not have the Pile do well out of the two of us.

A correction: in Year 5, Clark's Vase should have gone to Reina for 61 (one over Graham's 60), not 62. Reina gets 1 back, Clark's quarter falls from 15.5 to 15, and the Harvest Pile's share from 46.5 to 46.

The Year 6 auctions, settled once more after the live raises: Reina's Customs House (minimum 5) to Silke for 23 (Clark stopped at 22, Paddy 18, Graham 16, Noah 15); Noah's Land Deed (minimum 365) unsold, so both Deeds stay in his cart; Graham's Brush (minimum 5) to Paddy for 22 (Clark raised to 21; Noah 15); Silke's Jar (minimum 10) to Paddy for 21 (Graham raised to 20; Noah 15); Paddy's Bowl (minimum 5) to Silke for 17 (Clark stopped at 16, Graham 13, Noah 12); Clark's Vase (minimum 10) to Paddy for 21 (Graham raised to 20; Noah 15). Reina, Noah, Graham, Clark and Rob win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.

Vase, Deed, Brush, Customs House, Bowl, and twenty grain. Five years of losing every lot, and then two years of winning the ones that mattered. Reina darling, you told Graham to count his thirty carefully, so I'll count yours: three hundred and ninety-one. I'll take the chair and the purse, thank you. The coast is yours now, and the rent is five, and the sea air is very good for pottery.

Down the west edge in a column, Rob, where Graham kept his once, and nobody walked off with them in a year when your lads are on leave. I need one Dragon Jar, and there happen to be two in my old cart. Paddy, you're the Silk Peasant now, so I'll be bidding on your Jars, and I'll pay a fair price for one in public.

Three pieces for sixty-four grain, and I'm not sure I've ever had a better day at market. They're going in a row at the back by the paddies, Rob, well away from the sand, so you can tell your lads not to bother.

Placed: Silke's Customs House on M25 and Bowl on N25; Paddy's Brush on S19 and Jar on S20. Then SILKE TAKES REINA'S SEAT. She shows the Silk Peasant's complete set (Vase, Land Deed Scroll, Bamboo Brush, Customs House, Wooden Bowl) and replaces Reina as the Official, in Province 2. She keeps her 60 and takes all of Reina's 391 (451 in all). Her Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock; her Vase, Deed, Brush and Bowl move to G13-G16. Reina returns her Bowl, Brush, Jar and Vase to stock, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Silk Peasant, in Province 5; the two Jars in Province 5's stock are hers to sell. Silke now collects the tax; her new objective is a Dragon Jar and 20 grain. Then Clark's Vase goes to Paddy for 21, on S21. Paddy now holds a Brush, Jar and Vase.
Reina, not Paddy, is the Silk Peasant now; the two Jars in Province 5's stock are hers to sell. Silke holds 451.

Down the west edge in a column, Silke? Where Graham kept his? Darling, that's the most famous shop window in China. W2 is two steps from every piece you own, and he's only on leave for one more round. Paddy, I've already had a Jar off you, so you can stop hiding the Vase. I'm full up on paddy pottery.

Rob marches without raiding (his disaster): W1 to I11 and W3 to L22, both already raided; W2, W4 and W5 stand still. Then Rich pays the salaries: 8 to Silke, the new Official, and 6 to Graham, the Scholar. Year 6 ends. The seats now: Rich Emperor, Silke Official, Noah Gentry, Graham Scholar, Reina Silk Peasant, Paddy Rice Peasant, Clark Wheat Peasant, Rob Warlord.

Imperial Charity. Moved by the suffering of his people, the Emperor opens his purse. Slightly." Every province gets an average harvest, and every player gets two from the Emperor's reserve. Population holds at a hundred million, so that's times one; read the x1 row. No disasters this year. And Rich, since we're on charity: the Scholar's salary is five at the least, and that would be five on top of the two.

Graham reads the card: Imperial Charity. An average harvest for every province, the population holds at x1, and Rich gives every player 2 from the reserve (14 in all). Noah pays out the average harvest.

Average harvest all round, so here's the sum. Thirty-five each to Rich, Silke, Graham, Reina and me, fifty-five each to Paddy and Clark, and ten to Rob. That's two hundred and ninety-five out of the Pile, which leaves five hundred and thirty-three. Rent stays at five, same as last year: Reina, Paddy, Clark, five each please. And Paddy, I've still got two Deeds in the cart and I still owe you a favour, so when it's your turn come and talk to me about a fair price. I mean a fair one this time, not three hundred and sixty-five.
The Harvest Pile held 1123 before the harvest, so after paying out 295 it holds 828, not 533.
Noah keeps the rent at 5; Reina, Paddy and Clark pay him 5 each.

Storyteller's tip: 610 of the public works are still owed, and the game can't end until every one is built, one project a year. Five of the twenty I Ching cards raise the population and none has come up yet; each one makes every province hungrier.
Your 152 already included the harvest's 35, so the 15 in rent took you to 167.

Thirty percent, my friends. Moderate, civilised and not a grain more, as always. Graham, your five is eight, minus the two the card already handed you, so call it six and a warm smile. And this year the crown digs both canal sections through Province 5, all eighty at my own expense. Reina, your harvest is twenty a year fatter from today. Think of it as a gift from a grateful sovereign to the lady who once held his fields.

Rich declares the tax at 30%, builds both Grand Canal sections in Reina's Province 5 at the crown's cost (80), and will pay salaries of 8 to the Official, Silke, and 6 to the Scholar, Graham, at the end of the year.
A canal section adds its 10 from the next harvest on, so Reina's harvest grows by 20 from Year 8.

Thirty percent it is, and I'll put mine in first so nobody says the collector skimmed. Ten and a half from me, Noah, Graham and Reina; sixteen and a half from Paddy and Clark. Seventy-five on the nail, Your Majesty, counted twice. And Rob, I'll ask you politely, once, in front of witnesses. And Rich, thank you for the eight. I'll be keeping the receipt.

Silke collects the 30% tax, 75 in all, for the crown; Rob refuses his 3. Rich digs both canal sections in Province 5 (80). Works still owed: 530. Now the auctions: Silke sells a Customs House, Noah a Land Deed, Graham a Brush, Reina a Dragon Jar, Paddy a Bowl, Clark a Vase.

Ten for my Customs House, and it's cheap at that. Everyone knows which lot I'm sitting up for, so I'll say it plainly: I want Reina's Jar, and anyone who wants to make me pay for it is pouring their own grain into Noah's Pile to do it. Reina, the sea air must have done wonders for your pottery.

First, I got two sums wrong a minute ago, and the Storyteller's right on both: the Pile is eight hundred and twenty-eight, and I was on a hundred and sixty-seven before the tax. I'm on a hundred and fifty-six and a half now. My Deed's minimum is eight, Paddy, and that's the fair price I promised you. I'm not standing in Silke's way on the Jar either. Nobody here can outbid four hundred and eighty-five, and trying would only feed the Pile.

Six and a warm smile, Rich. I'll take the six, and I'll write the smile down at its market value. The Brush opens at six. As for the Jar, Silke, it's yours. I've learned what it costs to argue with four hundred and eighty-five, and I've already paid that lesson once.

Silke darling, nobody's standing in your way, and I wouldn't dream of it. The Jar opens at a hundred and fifty. The sea air is lovely, but it doesn't pay for itself, and you did walk off with three hundred and ninety-one of mine. Call it the civilised conversation I promised you, settled in public with the minutes as witness. As for everyone else, I'm only shopping for the cheap pieces this year. I'm starting again from the bottom, and the bottom is a very good place to plan from.

Eight's a fair price, Noah, and I'll hold you to the spirit of it, even if the lads with deeper pockets don't. I'll be honest with the table, since I can't hide it: I'm after the Customs House and the Deed, and nothing else. My Bowl opens at five, and it's a good honest bowl, Reina, if you're shopping from the bottom.

For the minutes: I'm still out of the Jars, since my promise stands until Noah has one again. Paddy, here's a deal in public so nobody feeds the Pile. You have Noah's Deed at his fair eight and I won't lift a finger, and I take the Customs House. If you bid against me on it anyway, that goes in my ledger, and you've seen the size of my ledger. My Vase opens at ten, and it's a modest price from a modest wheat farmer.
Not a grain from the desert this year, friends. Graham, Reina, the cheap pieces are going for a song. Buy something nice and put it somewhere I can admire it. I'll be along to have a look.

That's a fair offer, Clark, and I'll shake on it with one small addition so neither of us ends up a piece short. You take the Customs House today and I take the Deed. Next year you leave the next Customs House to me and I leave Noah's last Deed to you. That way we both finish, and none of it goes into the Pile.

Done, Paddy, and shaken on in front of witnesses. The Customs House is mine today, the Deed is yours, and next year we swap. I'm writing it on a fresh page headed 'Paddy, settled', which is the first page in that ledger that isn't a grievance.

The Year 7 auctions, settled from the limits (no lot close enough for a live raise): Silke's Customs House (minimum 10) to Clark for 15 (Graham stopped at 14, Reina 14, Noah 12; Paddy stood aside, as agreed); Noah's Land Deed Scroll (minimum 8) to Paddy for 15 (Graham stopped at 14, Reina 12; Clark stood aside, as agreed); Graham's Bamboo Brush (minimum 6) to Clark for 13 (Reina stopped at 12, Noah 10); Reina's Dragon Jar (minimum 150) to Silke for 150, unopposed; Paddy's Wooden Bowl (minimum 5) to Clark for 17 (Graham stopped at 16, Reina 12, Noah 10); Clark's Vase (minimum 10) to Graham for 16 (Reina stopped at 15, Noah 10). Rob passed on everything; Reina and Noah win nothing. Each seller keeps a quarter; three quarters go to the Harvest Pile.

With the Jar, Silke holds the Official's complete set (Vase, Land Deed Scroll, Bamboo Brush, Wooden Bowl, Dragon Jar) after the fourth lot, with 339 grain. The two lots after it (Paddy's Bowl to Clark, Clark's Vase to Graham) complete nobody's set.

A hundred and fifty, Reina, and worth every grain. Consider your three hundred and ninety-one avenged at a fair discount. Vase, Deed, Brush, Bowl and Jar: Rich, I believe you're sitting in my chair. The weaver's at the top table now, and she'll keep her promises to the letter, just as she was taught.

Silke places the Jar on G12, then SILKE TAKES THE THRONE. She shows the Official's complete set (Vase, Land Deed Scroll, Bamboo Brush, Wooden Bowl, Dragon Jar) and replaces Rich as Emperor, in Province 1. She keeps her 339 and takes Rich's whole reserve, 261.5 (600.5 in all), and returns all five pieces to stock. Rich holds nothing, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Official, in Province 2: he collects the tax from next year. Then lots 5 and 6 settle as above: Clark takes the Bowl and Graham the Vase.
Thank you, Noah, that was fair, and thank you, Clark, for keeping your word. The Deed goes on R22, well back from the shore. I learned that lesson the hard way, and I paid for it with a Jar.

Fifteen, thirteen and seventeen: three pieces for forty-five grain, and not one of them won by one. I'm putting them on the back row, Rob, so you'll have to admire them from a long way off. Congratulations, Your Majesty Silke. I'll be checking whether the new crown builds a link over Province 7, for the minutes.

Sixteen for a Vase. Two years ago one cost me sixty-one and I didn't even get it. Clark, thank you; it's going on J19, as far back as Province 4 goes. Rob, you're welcome to admire it from the desert.

Placed: Clark's Customs House on S15, Brush on S16 and Bowl on S17; Paddy's Land Deed on R22; Graham's Vase on J19. Paddy now holds a Brush, Jar, Vase and Deed and needs only a Customs House; Clark holds a Customs House, Brush and Bowl.
The Great Wall runs only above Provinces 1, 2 and 3, so no link can be built over Province 7.
A peasant with a full set may take the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat, or another peasant's, but never the throne directly.

Congratulations, Your Majesty Silke, and commiserations, Rich. The chair goes round faster than the gravy, I did say so. Graham, that Vase on J19 is lovely, and I've decided to admire it from closer up. Reina, Rich, a small visit each, just to keep the habit.

Rob marches and every soldier raids: W1 onto J12 and W2 onto H15 (Rich pays 5 each), W3 onto K21 (Graham pays 5), W4 onto P24 and W5 onto P20 (Reina pays 5 each). Then the salaries: Silke, the Emperor at year's end, pays what Rich declared, 8 to Rich as the Official and 6 to Graham as the Scholar. Year 7 ends.

Heaven Has Favourites. Some fields shine, some fields sulk." Provinces 2, 4 and 5 have a good harvest. Provinces 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8 have a bad one. The population holds at a hundred million, times one, so read the x1 row. No disasters this year. Your Majesty Silke, the Scholar's salary is five at the least, and your predecessor's habit was six.
Graham reads the card: Heaven Has Favourites. A good harvest in Provinces 2, 4 and 5, a bad one in 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8; the population holds at x1. Noah pays out the harvest.

Two hundred and eighty out of the Pile this year. Eighty to Reina, sixty each to Rich and Graham, thirty each to Paddy and Clark, ten to Her Majesty and ten to me, and nothing for the desert. Rent's five again, the same as every year: Reina, Paddy, Clark, five each please. Congratulations, Your Majesty. You'll find this table doesn't leave a full purse alone for long, and I'm saying that as a man who's lost two of them.
Noah keeps the rent at 5; Reina, Paddy and Clark pay him 5 each.

Forty percent, my friends. The crown has a wall, two palaces and a great deal of canal to keep up, and I've seen what this table does to a thin purse. Graham, both canal sections through Province 4 are on me, eighty grain, so that's twenty a year more for the Scholar. Six to each of my officers. Rich, the job pays exactly what you paid me for it, and I think that's fair.

Silke declares the tax at 40%, offers to build both Grand Canal sections in Graham's Province 4 at the crown's whole cost (80), and will pay salaries of 6 to the Official, Rich, and 6 to the Scholar, Graham, at the end of the year.
Rich paid Silke 8 a year as the Official, not 6.
A peasant with a full set may take the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat, but never the throne directly.

Forty percent, Your Majesty, and collected with the greatest pleasure. I'll put mine in first, as you once did: twenty-four from me, twenty-four from Graham, thirty-two from Reina, twelve each from Paddy and Clark, and four from Noah. That's a hundred and eight on the nail, counted twice. Rob, I'll ask you politely too, once, in front of witnesses. And Your Majesty, a small point for the minutes: I paid you eight, not six. I don't need to remind a sovereign who keeps her promises to the letter that the letter said eight.

Rich collects the 40% tax, 108 in all, for the crown; Rob's income is 0, so he owes nothing. Now the auctions: Rich sells a Customs House, Noah a Land Deed, Graham a Brush, Reina a Dragon Jar, Paddy a Bowl, Clark a Vase. The Emperor doesn't bid.

My Customs House opens at ten, the same honest price Her Majesty set last year, and Paddy, I believe you've a gentleman's agreement that makes it yours. For my part, a humble Official starting from the bottom will bid a modest grain here and there and never two where one will do. I'll feed no one's Pile with my pride, Noah, you can count it.

Rich, for the minutes: you collected a hundred and eight and I paid four of it. I won't argue with the most honest number I've paid all game. I'm staying out of the Customs House, because Paddy and Clark shook on it and I won't be the man who makes a handshake expensive. The Deed's at eight again, Clark, and that's the same fair price Paddy paid. Everything else, I'll pay eighteen and not a grain more. Last year I lost three lots at ten, so I've learned that much.

I accept the canal, Your Majesty, with thanks, and I'll note it was the first gift from the crown that came without a receipt attached. I'm not part of anyone's handshake, so I'll bid my own figures on everything I need and drop out when they're reached. The Brush opens at six again.
Graham agrees: Silke digs both Grand Canal sections in Province 4 at the crown's whole cost (80). Works still owed: 450.
A peasant with a full set may take the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat, but never the throne directly.

Paddy darling, I can count to five as well as anyone. A Brush, a Jar, a Vase and a Deed, and Rich's Customs House would finish the set, with six hundred and twenty-four grain in Her Majesty's reserve waiting at the end of it. Your handshake was with Clark, not with me, so if you want that chair you'll pay a proper price for it in front of witnesses. Everything else I'm bidding on honestly, from the bottom up, and the Jar opens at twenty for anyone who's still collecting.

A peasant with a full set can't take the throne, so the Emperor's reserve isn't within Paddy's reach. He could take the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat, or another peasant's, and that player's grain.

Thank you, Rich, and thank you, Noah, for leaving a handshake alone. Reina, you're right, you weren't in on it, and I won't pretend you were. If you want to push me on that Customs House, push away, but every grain we throw at it goes into the Pile, and only a quarter goes to Rich. I'm not bidding on anything else this year, and my Bowl opens at five.

For the minutes: I'm out of the Customs House as Paddy and I shook, and I'm still out of the Jar, because my word was to stay out until Reina and Noah each had one. Noah, it's yours at eighteen with my blessing. Reina, you can't buy your own Jars, so I'd ask you to release me in public once Noah has his. The Deed I'm bidding on honestly, and my Vase opens at ten.

The desert passes again, friends. Rich, Reina, you're both shopping from the bottom, and I'm rooting for you. Buy something lovely and put it on show. Graham, give my regards to that Vase. Someone will be by to see it shortly.

The first Year 8 lot: Rich's Customs House (minimum 10) to Paddy for 51. Graham stopped at 15; Reina went to 50 to keep it from Paddy; Clark and Noah stood aside, as promised. With it Paddy holds the Rice Peasant's complete set, with 55 grain. The other lots wait on what he does with it.

Fifty-one grain, Reina, and you made me earn every one of them, which is fair enough. Here it is: Brush, Jar, Vase, Deed and Customs House, the whole set, and from a rice farmer who came home with an empty cart in Year One. Noah, you've been fair with me all game and I'm sorry it's you, but you did say you owed me a favour. I'll run the Pile honestly, and rent stays at five while I'm the one asking for it.

Paddy places the Customs House on S22, then PADDY TAKES NOAH'S SEAT. He shows the Rice Peasant's complete set (Bamboo Brush, Dragon Jar, Vase, Land Deed Scroll, Customs House) and replaces Noah as the Gentry, in Province 3. He keeps his 55 and takes Noah's 181 (236 in all). His Deed goes back to Province 3's stock, which he now sells; his Brush, Jar, Vase and Customs House move with him to Province 3. Noah holds nothing, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Rice Peasant, in Province 6; Province 6's Bowls are his to sell. Paddy now pays out the harvest and asks the rent; his new objective is a Wooden Bowl and 20 grain.

The rest of the Year 8 lots, settled from the same limits (none of Noah's is above the 60 he now holds): Paddy's (formerly Noah's) Land Deed to Clark for 19 (Graham stopped at 18, Reina 16, Rich 14); Graham's Brush, Reina 19 against Noah 18: close; Reina's Jar to Graham for 21 (Rich and Noah stopped at 20); Noah's (formerly Paddy's) Bowl, Graham 20 against Reina 20, Graham ahead by seat order: close; Clark's Vase to Reina for 19 (Noah stopped at 18, Rich 14). The two close lots get one live raise each.

Four pieces in a row on M10 to M13, well back from the desert. Rob, you can admire them through a telescope. Noah, the Bowls are yours to sell now, and they're good ones. I should know, I've been selling them for eight years.

Well. I learned something about the rules this year, and it cost me fifty grain, which is about my usual rate. Noah darling, I'm sorry, and I'm sorry it was my push that put the sums in front of him. I'm not leaving empty-handed twice, though. Twenty-four for the Brush and twenty-six for the Bowl, and then I'll stop, I promise.

I said eighteen and not a grain more, so it's yours, Reina. Paddy, there's nothing to apologise for. I told you I owed you a favour, and the arithmetic says I've just paid it at a hundred and eighty-one grain, which is about a hundred and sixty more than I'd planned. That's the third time I've been caught sitting on a full purse with nothing in hand, and I've only got myself to blame.
I've lost two lots at twenty against twenty-one, Reina, both of them in the last two years. I'm not losing a third by a single grain. Twenty-six.
Reina lost the Customs House to Paddy and paid nothing for it: only the winner of a lot pays.

After the live raises: Graham's Brush to Reina for 19 (Noah held at 18; Reina had raised to 24); Noah's Bowl to Graham for 26 (Reina also raised to 26; Graham keeps it by seat order). So the Year 8 lots: Customs House to Paddy 51, Land Deed to Clark 19, Brush to Reina 19, Jar to Graham 21, Bowl to Graham 26, Vase to Reina 19. Paddy's pieces move to M10-M13 in Province 3.

Nineteen for the Deed, and won by one this time, Graham, so that page of mine finally has an entry going the other way. It goes on S14 beside its brothers. Noah, my condolences; you've been the fairest man at this table, and I've written that under 'admired' too.

I stand corrected, and happily so: it cost me nothing but my pride, and pride's the one thing this table never runs short of. A Brush and a Vase for thirty-eight, Rob, and I've put them right down at the bottom corner of the coast, as far back as Province 5 goes. Graham, twenty-six for the Bowl is a fair price, and I won't grudge you a single grain of it.

The Jar goes on K24 and the Bowl on K19, beside the Vase at the back. Reina, twenty-six against twenty-six, and the seat order went my way for once. I'm not going to apologise for the one time it did.

Placed: Paddy's Customs House on S23 (S22 had been raided), then moved with his pieces to M10-M13; Clark's Deed on S14; Reina's Brush on M25 and Vase on L25; Graham's Jar on K24 and Bowl on K19. Clark now needs only a Dragon Jar; Graham needs a Customs House and a Deed; Paddy, as the Gentry, needs a Wooden Bowl.

Congratulations, Paddy. You put four pieces back where my lads can't reach them, and I respect a man who learns. Graham, Reina, you've got such lovely things now, and you've put them so far from the sea. Lucky for me the desert isn't by the sea. Noah, bad luck, mate. The chair goes round faster than the gravy.

Rob marches and every soldier raids: W1 onto K12 (Paddy pays 5), W2 onto H16 (Rich pays 5), W3 onto K20 (Graham pays 5), W4 onto O24 and W5 onto P21 (Reina pays 5 each). Then Silke pays the salaries she declared, 6 to Rich and 6 to Graham. Year 8 ends.

A new house rule, from Year 9: a lot that goes unsold at its minimum must be offered again the next round, the same piece, with the minimum at 2. A seller may hold a piece back for one round, never two in a row.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." The counter stays at one hundred million, times one, so read the first row of your tables, everyone, the bad-year column. No province is named, so nobody opens their disaster booklet this year. Paddy, the Pile has eight hundred and seventy-six in it. I expect we'll all be very polite to you this spring.

Right so, a bad year all round, and here's the harvest as the tables have it: ten to Silke, Rich and myself, thirty each to Graham, Reina, Noah and Clark, and nothing to Rob. Rent's five apiece, the same as I promised, and it'll stay at five while I'm in this chair. Noah, I've not forgotten you were always fair with me, and I'd sooner pay an honest price for one of your Bowls than see either of them sit beside the board all year.

Storyteller's tip: 450 of the public works are still owed, in four projects at the fastest (all eight Wall links built in one year count as one project), so the game can't end before Year 12. None of the five I Ching cards that raise the population has come up yet, and each one makes every province hungrier.

Rotten seed and a lame ox. I've worked those fields myself, so the crown takes twenty this year and not a grain more. Rich, your four Wall links go up this spring and the crown pays for every stone. Nobody at this table will say I sat on the reserve while the north stood open. Graham, there's two extra for reading us such a cheerful card.

Silke declares a tax of 20%, salaries of 6 to the Official and 8 to the Scholar, and this year's one project: all four links of the Great Wall above Province 2, the crown paying the whole 160. A Wall over Province 2 is negotiated with that province, so Rich, as its holder, is asked to agree.

Twenty percent in a rotten year. Your Majesty is mercy itself, and Province 2 accepts its Wall with deep thanks. Two from me, two from Paddy, six each from Graham, Reina, Noah and Clark, twenty-eight for the crown, and I'll count every grain of it in front of you all. Rob, I'll ask anyway, because asking is my job. And Majesty, I see six beside my name and eight beside Graham's. I'm not complaining. I'm only writing it down.

Rich collects 28 at 20% (Rob's income is 0) and agrees to the Wall. Silke builds all four links of the Great Wall above Province 2, the crown paying the whole 160. Works still owed: 290, in four projects: the Wall above Province 3 (four links, 160, negotiated with Paddy), the Province 2 Irrigation System (30, negotiated with Rich), the Province 3 Reservoir (80, negotiated with Paddy), and the Marble Pagoda (20), built in a year when nothing else is.

My Customs House goes up at two, friends. I'm a humble collector now and I've no use for a toll gate on an empty road. As for the rest, I'll bid like a man with a hundred and fifteen grain and five empty shelves, which means politely and never far. Clark, I won't fight you for that Jar. A man one piece from his set has earned a clear road, and I'd like to be remembered as the one who stood aside.
Clark is a peasant, so a full set would let him replace the Official, the Gentry, the Scholar or another peasant, never the Emperor.

I'll be honest with you all, because I don't know how to be anything else. I want one thing at this market and that's Noah's Bowl, and I'll stay out of every other lot so nobody's pushed up on my account. My Deed goes up at two for whoever wants it. Rich, Reina, if either of you fancies that Bowl, I'd much rather we talk about it now than pour the both of our purses into the Pile.
The Emperor doesn't bid at auction, so Silke can't bid on any lot.

Rich, Paddy, thank you both for starting at two. I'll be honest too, since everyone else is: I'm bidding on the Customs House and the Deed and nothing else. Anyone who wants either of them should know I've written my figure down, and I won't be talked off it this time. My Brush goes up at two. Somebody take it home.

Paddy darling, I won't pour grain into the Pile over a Bowl. Noah has two, so you take one and I'll take the other, and neither of us goes past thirty. Clark, my Jar opens at a hundred. That's what a full set and a seat are worth, and you can do those sums better than anyone.

Here's my arithmetic, out loud as usual: eighty-five and a half grain, five empty shelves, so it's fourteen to sixteen on each lot and not a grain past it. Graham, if your written figure's over fourteen, the Customs House is yours and I'll clap. Reina, a hundred for a Jar is a seat's price and I haven't got a seat's purse, so that one's Clark's problem. My Bowl goes up at eight. Paddy, that's your honest price, and if Reina wants the other one it's eight for her too.

For the minutes: Noah just called the Jar 'Clark's problem' in front of eight witnesses, and Reina put it up for sale to me by name.
