I'll take that as my public release, and it's noted and carried forward that I stood out of the Jars for five years. Reina, a hundred's a steep price for a pot, and I'll pay it to you rather than wait for the new house rule to hand it to me at two next spring. Rich, standing aside goes in the ledger under 'admired', right next to Noah's Deed. My Vase opens at twelve, which is cheaper than it's ever been, and it's the last one I'll sell.
The Emperor doesn't bid at auction, so Silke can't bid against anyone. And the game has no fixed last year: it ends when every public work owed is built.

Third year running the desert sits on its hands, friends. Go on, bid each other up, fill the Pile, and buy yourselves something nice. Rich especially. A man with five empty shelves is a man I can't visit, and I do hate to leave anyone off my rounds. Graham, that Bowl on K19 is lovely. I can see it from here. Well, W3 can.

The first two Year 9 lots: Rich's Customs House to Graham for 51 (Noah stopped at 14, Reina at 50 to keep it from him); Paddy's Land Deed to Graham for 31 (Noah 14, Rich 16, Reina 30). Graham now holds a Vase, Jar, Bowl, Customs House and Land Deed: the Scholar's full set, with 60.5 grain. The other lots wait on what he does.

Vase, Jar, Bowl, Customs House, Deed. That's five pieces in the hall and sixty and a half grain in hand, and I'm showing it before anyone else gets to the next lot. Your Majesty, you were kind to me about the canal and the two extra, and I mean it when I say this isn't a grievance. I've just learned what happens to a man who keeps his set in a drawer for one more round. I'll take the throne.

Graham places the Customs House on K23 and the Deed on L23, then GRAHAM TAKES THE THRONE. He shows the Scholar's complete set and 60.5 grain and replaces Silke as Emperor, taking her whole reserve of 490.5 (551 in all); all five pieces go back to stock. Silke, who holds nothing, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Scholar, in Province 4; the next lot, Province 4's last Brush, is hers to sell. The later lots are settled from the same limits: lot 3, the Brush, to Rich for 17 (Noah stopped at 16); lot 4, Reina's Jar, to Clark for 100, its minimum. With the Jar Clark holds the Wheat Peasant's full set (Customs House, Brush, Bowl, Deed, Jar) with 61.5 grain.

Customs House, Brush, Bowl, Deed, and Reina's Jar on S13: five pieces on the back row and sixty-one and a half grain, so I'm showing it now. Paddy, it's not a grievance, it's arithmetic: you were one Bowl away from that same chair, and I've just watched Graham teach the whole table what one more round costs. Your page in my ledger stays headed 'Paddy, settled', and I'll keep the rent at five, same as you promised.

Clark places the Jar on S13, then CLARK TAKES PADDY'S SEAT. He shows the Wheat Peasant's complete set and 61.5 grain and replaces Paddy as the Gentry, in Province 3, taking Paddy's 266 (327.5 in all). His Deed goes back to Province 3's stock, which he now sells; his Customs House, Brush, Bowl and Jar move with him to Province 3. Paddy returns his four pieces to stock, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Wheat Peasant, in Province 7; Province 7's last Vase, the sixth lot, is his to sell. Clark now pays the harvest and asks the rent; as the Gentry he needs a Vase and 20 grain. The last two lots, settled from the same limits (Paddy's cut to the 60 he now holds): lot 5, Noah's Bowl, to Paddy for 31 (Rich stopped at 14, Reina at 30); lot 6, the Vase, to Rich for 17 (Noah stopped at 16).

Two thrones and one Gentry's chair changed hands before the pots were cold, and here I am with a Brush and a Vase for seventeen apiece. Congratulations, Your Majesty Graham, and congratulations, Clark. Silke, Paddy, I know exactly how that floor feels, and you'll both get up again. Rob, both pieces sit tucked under my new Wall, so you'll have to admire them from a distance.
One throne changed hands this year, Graham's, and one Gentry's seat, Clark's.

Paddy left me a nice clean row on M, and I'm not using it, because Rob's W1 is sitting on K12 two steps away and I've already had one Deed carried off to a dune. Back corner, H9 to I9, same as always. Rob, you'll have to admire them from a distance, like Rich said. Paddy, rent's five, it stays five, and you'll have your harvest from me on time.
Clark's pieces go to H9 (Customs House), H11 (Bowl), and, since H10 and I9 have been raided, I8 (Brush) and J9 (Jar), the nearest legal squares in his corner.

Well. I came to market one Bowl short of a full set and I'm going home with one Bowl and no set at all, so I suppose that's what they mean by a lesson. Congratulations, Clark, you earned it fair and in front of everyone, which is more than I can say for how I've felt about it these last five minutes. Noah, thank you for the honest price, even if I paid a bit over it.

Placed: Rich's Brush on G12 and Vase on H12; Paddy's Bowl on S16. The Year 9 lots in all: Customs House to Graham 51, Deed to Graham 31, Brush to Rich 17, Jar to Clark 100, Bowl to Paddy 31, Vase to Rich 17.

Congratulations, Your Majesty Graham. Congratulations, Clark. Two new chairs in one market, and you both left me a lovely trail of pots to follow. Rich, you said I'd have to admire your Brush and Vase from a distance, and you're right, the distance is three steps. W1 and W2 send their regards. Reina, W4 is two steps from your bottom corner and he's wiped his boots.
From the board: W4 is one step from Reina's Brush on M25 and two from her Vase; W1 is two from Rich's Vase and three from his Brush.

Rob marches, and every soldier raids for 5: W1 onto J11 (Clark pays), W2 onto G15 (Rich), W3 onto J21 (Silke), W4 onto N24 and W5 onto O22 (Reina pays 10). Then Graham, the Emperor at year end, pays the salaries Silke declared: 6 to Rich and 8 to Silke, now the Scholar. Year 9 ends.

Storms and Raiders. A fine crop, and a fine season for gales, bandits and the Warlord's sense of humour. Every province collects a good harvest. Provinces 4, 5, 6 and 7 each pay two million to repair their public works, and that includes me, so I'm reading my own bill. Provinces 1, 2 and 3, and Rob, each play the next personal disaster in your booklet. The counter stays at one hundred million, times one, so everyone reads the first row of your tables, good-year column. Your Majesty, I hope the throne is comfortable. I warmed it for you myself, and I'll take my five at year's end, or more if you remember the canal.
The pieces returned to stock in Year 9 are on sale again: every seller from Province 2 to 7 has at least one piece to auction this year.

Clark pays out a good harvest. Then the repairs: Silke, Reina, Noah and Paddy each pay 2 to the Harvest Pile. The disasters: Graham's Prince breaks an ivory figure (10); Rich pays for a barge that rammed a lock gate (10); Clark refurnishes a house stripped by thieves (10); and Rob wakes from a riding accident to find half his wealth stolen by his own men (128.5). Grain now: Graham 587, Clark 372.5, Reina 221, Noah 171, Rich 145, Silke 145, Rob 138.5, Paddy 111; pile 609.

Harvest paid in full, every grain where the tables put it, and Rob, that twenty's yours. It's the first entry on your page that goes the other way. Rent's five apiece, the same as Paddy promised and the same as I promised, and I've written it in the ledger where you can all check it. Your Majesty Graham, five hundred and eighty-seven is a very handsome reserve, and I'm sure you'll want to start on the two hundred and ninety of works with it.

Thirty percent in a good year, so a hundred and thirty-two if everyone pays. Rich, eight to you, and Silke, eight to you for the canal and the card. Nobody at this table gets docked for doing an honest job while I'm in this chair, because I know exactly what it costs. Clark, the crown will build Province 3 its Reservoir and pay all eighty, if you'll have it. I'll tell you plainly I'd sooner pay for your furrows than have you counting mine.

Graham declares a tax of 30%, salaries of 8 to the Official and 8 to the Scholar, and this year's one project: the Province 3 Reservoir, the crown paying the whole 80. It is negotiated with Province 3, so Clark, as its holder, is asked to agree.

Thirty percent in a good year, the same rate I kept for six years running, so I can hardly call it anything but moderate. Eighteen from me and from Clark, twenty-four each from Silke, Reina, Noah and Paddy, a hundred and thirty-two for the crown, counted out on the table where everyone can see. Rob, I'll ask, you'll refuse, and I'll write it down. And Your Majesty, eight is eight. Thank you for saying so before I had to.

Rich collects 132 at 30% for the crown; Rob refuses his 6. The auctions: Rich sells Province 2's Customs Houses, Clark the Deeds, Silke the last Brush, Reina the Jars, Noah the Bowls and Paddy the Vases. Graham, the Emperor, doesn't bid.
With your auction reply, please say whether you accept the crown's Reservoir, and name where its cut-out goes: two squares by three, on six free squares of Province 3 (for example K14:L16).

Customs Houses at two again, friends, and I'd be glad to see them go to good homes. I'll bid on a thing or two the way I always do, a grain over and never two. Your Majesty, a fine reserve you have there. I've always said the throne was the seat nobody wanted, and I meant it kindly.

Your Majesty, Province 3 accepts its Reservoir with thanks, and it goes on K14 to L16, and it's the first work ever built over one of my provinces, so that's a new line in a new column. The Deeds go at two; Paddy taught me that and I've written it down. I'll be honest the way everyone at this table has learned to be: I want one Vase, nothing else, and I'll stay out of every other lot so nobody's pushed up on my account.

A hundred and twenty-one grain and five empty shelves. I've been at this table with less, and I started out with one Vase and twenty-six grain, so don't feel sorry for me. My Brush goes up at two, and whoever takes it home gets a fine piece cheap. I'll bid on everything else like a weaver buying thread, at a fair price and not a grain past it, unless someone's three pieces from a chair. Then I'll get expensive.

Three pieces this market, darlings, and I'm not shy about it: the Customs House, a Deed and a Bowl, and I'll go above your fourteens and sixteens to get them. Clark, you sold me nothing and I sold you a seat, so the minutes say you owe me a civilised Deed. Nobody else needs my Jars, so they go up at ten for whoever fancies a pot.

I'll do the sum out loud, as I always do. All five of the pieces I need are on sale this year. I've a hundred and forty-two, the set needs twenty kept back, so that leaves a hundred and twenty-two to spread over five lots, about twenty-four each. If I win the lot, I'll show it. If anyone outbids me on even one, I'm a rice farmer with a full purse again, and you've all seen how that ends. Bowl's at eight, same honest price as last year.

Eighty-two grain and one Bowl in the sand, so I'm back where I started in Year One, only a bit wiser, I hope. I'll bid small and honest on the four I need and stay out of the Bowls altogether. My Vases go up at two, Rich, Noah, whoever wants one. And Clark, five's a fair rent, thank you for keeping it.

Half my tent walked off in the night with my own lads' boots on, so the desert's in no mood to shop. Go on, Silke, buy yourself a pot or two. A Scholar with empty shelves looks so lonely, and I'd love an excuse to pay you a visit. Clark, thank you for the twenty. I'll frame it.
Rich, Silke, Noah and Paddy all still need a Dragon Jar.

Reina took my Customs House and my Deed, so I can't finish the set this year whatever I pay for a Brush. I'll stand at the twenty I wrote down. If that's enough on seat order, I'll take it home, and if Paddy wants to go past it, it's his, and fairly bought.

Noah, you've lost the Customs House and the Deed already, so your set's not coming this year whatever happens with this Brush. I'll go a bit higher on it, and I'm sorry, because you've always given me an honest price.

After the live raise, Silke's Brush goes to Paddy for 21 (Noah held at 20). Lot 4, Reina's Jar, to Rich for 26 (Paddy stopped at 15, Silke 24, Noah 25); lot 5, Noah's Bowl, to Reina for 33 (Silke 30, Rich 32). With the Customs House, Deed and Bowl, Reina holds the Silk Peasant's full set (Brush, Vase, Customs House, Deed, Bowl) with 95.5 grain. The last lot waits on what she does.

Brush, Vase, Customs House, Deed and Bowl, all five on my coast, and I'm showing them before the last Vase goes under the hammer. Clark darling, you taught me what one more round costs, and I was paying attention. It's a very civilised conversation, and the minutes will say you started it.

Reina places the Customs House on L24, the Deed on O20 and the Bowl on P26, then REINA TAKES CLARK'S SEAT. She shows the Silk Peasant's complete set and 95.5 grain and replaces Clark as the Gentry, in Province 3, taking his 379.5 (475 in all). Her Deed goes back to Province 3's stock; her Brush, Vase, Customs House and Bowl move with her to Province 3. Clark returns all his pieces to stock, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Silk Peasant, in Province 5; Province 5's Jars are his to sell. The last lot, settled from the same limits (Clark's 330 cut to the 60 he now holds): Paddy's Vase to Clark for 26 (Silke stopped at 18, Noah at 25). Reina now pays the harvest and asks the rent; as the Gentry she needs a Dragon Jar and 20 grain.

Twenty-one for the Brush, and thank you, Noah, that's twice now you've been decent about a lot I wanted. Congratulations, Reina. That's three new seats in two markets, and I'm starting to think the only safe chair at this table is the one nobody's looking at. Clark, welcome to the floor. It's not so bad down here once you stop expecting the ceiling.

A Jar for twenty-six, one grain over Noah, which is the only way I know how to bid. Congratulations, Reina darling, and Clark, I'm sorry. The seat moves fast at this table and none of us gets to keep it. Brush, Vase and now a Jar, all three tucked under the Wall, so Rob, you'll need a long walk.
Placed: Paddy's Brush on S17; Rich's Jar on J14.

Back to the M row, darlings. I built there in Year Three and it served me well, and Rob, it's a long walk from K12 now that you've moved on. Paddy, Rich, Noah, the rent stays five from me, written in the same ledger.
The rent is paid by the three peasants, Clark, Noah and Paddy; Rich, the Official, pays none.

Well. Four hundred and fifty-five grain, five pieces and a Gentry's chair, and Reina had them all off me between two lots. Reina darling, it was a very civilised conversation, and the minutes will say I started it and you finished it. I've written it on a page of its own, under 'admired', right beside Noah's Deed. Twenty-six for a Vase, Paddy, thank you; it's the only thing I own now, and it's going in the corner of the coast I've just inherited.
Clark held 379.5 when Reina took his seat; he holds 34 now, after the Vase.

Clark's Vase goes on L25 (L26 is outside Province 5). Reina's pieces stand on M9 to M12. The Year 10 lots in all: Customs House to Reina 29, Deed to Reina 41, Brush to Paddy 21, Jar to Rich 26, Bowl to Reina 33, Vase to Clark 26.

Congratulations, Reina darling. Back on the M row, two steps from W1, just the way you left it in Year Three. Rich, it isn't a long walk at all. W2 is two steps from your Jar, your Vase and your Brush, so you can pick which one you'll miss least. And Your Majesty Graham, W3 would like to see the Winter Palace. I hear it's lovely in the spring.

Rob marches, and every soldier raids: W1 onto K11 (Reina pays 5), W2 onto H14 (Rich pays 5), W3 across the north river onto I21 in Province 1 (Graham pays 10, and Rob pays him a 5 toll), W4 onto M24 and W5 onto O21 (Clark pays 10). W1 now stands two steps from Reina's row and W2 two from all three of Rich's pieces; W3 is one from the Winter Palace. Then Graham pays the salaries he declared, 8 to Rich and 8 to Silke. Year 10 ends.

Where the table stands: Graham is the Emperor (618 grain in the reserve); Rich the Official (111; holds a Brush, Vase and Jar, needs a Deed and a Bowl); Reina the Gentry (470; holds a Brush, Vase, Customs House and Bowl, needs a Dragon Jar); Silke the Scholar (134; holds nothing); Clark the Silk Peasant (24; holds a Vase); Noah the Rice Peasant (150; holds nothing); Paddy the Wheat Peasant (67.5; holds a Bowl and Brush); Rob the Warlord (163.5). Works still owed: 210 (the Wall above Province 3, the Province 2 Irrigation System and the Marble Pagoda). The population is still x1.

Population Grows by Half. The villages are noisier than they used to be." Good harvest everywhere. The counter now reads one hundred and fifty million, so that's times one and a half, everyone. Read the right row of your income table, and remember you'll be feeding half as many again. Your Majesty, the Scholar's ink isn't getting any cheaper either.

Harvest's out of the Pile, darlings: sixty to every field, forty to Rich, thirty to His Majesty and ten to Rob's dunes. Rent stays at five, as promised in the minutes, because a good year is no excuse to get greedy. Clark, Noah, Paddy, five each please, and nobody has any reason to sign anything this spring.

Thirty percent again, same as last year. A good harvest doesn't need a greedy tax either, and Reina has already said so in the minutes. The crown builds the Pagoda this year, twenty grain and nobody else's field. Rich, Silke, eight each again. I'd like it on the record that this throne has never docked a salary.
The Pagoda goes on G18, at the back under the Wall. It's a place to pray, so it should be somewhere quiet.

Thirty percent, Your Majesty, as moderate as ever, and I'm the first to pay it: twelve from me, eighteen each from Reina, Silke, Clark, Noah and Paddy. That's a hundred and two for the crown, counted out in front of everyone. Rob, I'll put your refusal in the minutes as usual. And thank you, Your Majesty, for the eight. A throne that never docks a salary is a throne I'm very glad to serve.

Rich collects 102 at 30% for the crown; Rob refuses his 3. Graham builds the Marble Pagoda on G18 for 20; 190 of the works are still owed: the Wall above Province 3 (160) and the Province 2 Irrigation System (30).

My Customs House opens at two, friends, and it's a bargain at any price. As for the rest, everyone knows me by now: a grain over and never two. Reina, Noah, I'm only after what I need, and I'll tell you so to your faces.

Thirty percent and a Pagoda, Your Majesty, I'll vote for both of those. I'm only shopping for one thing this spring and everyone at this table knows what it is, so Clark darling, I'd keep your Jar polished. The Deeds go up at two, as cheap as I've ever sold them, because the Gentry wants the land in somebody's hands.

The Scholar's Brush starts at ten. It's a good year, and the ink's worth more in a good year. As for the Jar, Reina, you know better than anyone what a Jar costs at this table, and I mean to remind you.

For the minutes: the silk farmer has sixty-one grain and a Vase, so I'm bidding like a man with sixty-one grain and a Vase, small and steady. My Jar opens at thirty, and Reina, darling, you of all people know what a Jar is worth to the person one piece short. That's not a grievance, it's a price.

Right, the sum out loud, same as last year. A hundred and eighty-seven, twenty kept back for the set, so a hundred and sixty-five over five lots. That's thirty-one apiece and a bit more on the Jar, and yes, thirty-one is one grain above what I'd call honest. The Bowl's yours at six to whoever wants it. And Reina, I know you only need that Jar and you've five hundred behind you. I can't outbid that, but I'm not handing it to you at the minimum either.

I'll say it plain so nobody's surprised later: I want a Customs House, a Deed and a Jar, and I'll bid fair on all three and no further. Thank you, Your Majesty, for not docking salaries, and Reina, the five's on the table. Vase goes up at two, and whoever wants it is welcome to it.

Pass, pass, pass, and pass on the rest as well. Buy away, all of you, the Pile could do with the exercise. Lovely spot for the Pagoda, Your Majesty, nice and quiet under the Wall. I'll say a prayer for your Winter Palace while I'm passing, since my lad's standing on its doorstep.

The auction, lots 1 to 4: Noah takes Rich's Customs House for 29 (Paddy stopped at 28, Silke 24, Clark 15); Rich takes Reina's Land Deed Scroll for 32 (Noah stopped at 31, Paddy 28, Silke 24, Clark 12); Noah takes Silke's Brush for 17 (Clark 16); Reina takes Clark's Dragon Jar for 71 (Silke stopped at 70, Noah 41).

The Jar goes on I8 under the Wall, darlings, and the set goes on the table: Brush, Vase, Customs House, Bowl and Jar. Rich, my dear, you bought my whole set one polite grain at a time in Year Two, and you were one Bowl away from doing it again, so I'll have the Official's chair back now, please, and the ledger that goes with it. Your Majesty, keep the throne warm. I can count to one auction.

Twenty-nine, seventeen and twenty-one, that's sixty-seven, so I'm on a hundred and twenty with three pieces in hand. And Rich, you beat me on the Deed by one grain again, a grain over and never two, just like you said. They're all going right down in the far corner of the paddies, Rob, so your lads will need a good long walk to reach them.

Reina shows the Gentry's set after lot 4 and takes Rich's seat as the Official, and his 114 (578 in all). Rich returns everything, draws 60 and is the Gentry now, in Province 3, selling the Deeds. Lot 5: Rich takes Noah's Wooden Bowl for 27 (Silke stopped at 26, Clark 12). Lot 6: Noah takes Paddy's Vase for 21 (Silke 20). Noah puts his Customs House, Brush and Vase on S23, S24 and S25.

Everything goes back up the province where Rich kept his, darlings: G12, H12, I12 and J14, tucked under the Wall. Rich, I've only borrowed your filing system, and I'll give it back in the same condition. All I need now is a Land Deed, and I know exactly who's selling them this year.

Well played, Reina, very well played. You took my chair the way I once took yours, so I can't call it a grievance. It's arithmetic, and it's my own arithmetic. The Bowl goes on J17, a long way from anybody's boots. Noah, Clark, Paddy: the rent stays at five, as it's written in the minutes. And the Deeds are still for sale at a fair price for anyone who wants land.
Reina puts her Brush, Vase, Bowl and Jar on G12, H12, I12 and J14; she needs only a Land Deed Scroll now, and Rich sells them. Rich puts the Bowl on J17.

Reina, darling, you've borrowed Rich's filing system and his shelf under the Wall, and you've borrowed his visitors too. Two of my lads will be round with the tea shortly. Your Majesty, W3 has come to admire your Winter Palace. It's even prettier up close.

Rob marches: W1 to J12 (already raided), W2 to I13 (Reina pays 5), W3 onto the Winter Palace on H21 (Graham pays 20; Rob counts the palace in place of one player's piece), W4 to L24 (Clark pays 5), W5 to N21 (Silke pays 5). Graham pays the salaries, 8 to Reina as the Official and 8 to Silke. End of Year 11: Graham 694, Reina 581, Rob 208.5, Silke 183, Noah 126.5, Paddy 109.5, Clark 73.5, Rich 33; pile 491. Works owed 190.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families." Good harvest everywhere, and the counter goes to three hundred million, which is times three, everyone. Use the times-three row, and check it twice before you eat, because every mouth at this table is now doubled. Rich, mind your Deeds. There's only one buyer who matters this spring.

Storyteller's tip: new land is open now, but Province 3's only new land is the strip below the Wall, and it opens only when all four Wall links above Province 3 stand. Those links (160) are one of the two works still owed, and the split is negotiated with the crown.

Harvest's out of the Pile, friends: the fields come out even this year, and His Majesty, Reina and Rob pay in what the times-three row says they owe. Rent is five each from Clark, Noah and Paddy, as it was in my old minutes and in Reina's, because a promise made in Year Two is still a promise. Your Majesty, there are four links of Wall over Province 3 waiting to be built, and the Gentry would be very glad to discuss how we share them.

Thirty percent of nothing is nothing, so the rate stays where it's always been. The crown pays fifteen of every twenty on new land, for every field at this table, and that includes the ones that don't like me. Rich, four links of Wall over your province for twenty of yours, and the crown puts in the other hundred and forty. Reina, Silke, eight each, as always.
The Wall's yours for twenty. All I'd ask is that a Deed doesn't go to Reina cheap this spring. Make her pay what my chair is worth.

Graham declares 30%, but no province has a positive income at x3, so no tax is owed. He offers Rich the Wall above Province 3, the crown paying 140 and Rich 20, buys six squares of new land for Province 1 (E16 to E21, 120), and says the crown pays 15 of every 20 on every other province's new squares this year.

Your Majesty, that's the most generous twenty I've ever been asked for, and I'm glad to pay it. Four links over Province 3, and since the crown is covering fifteen of every twenty, I'll take all three squares under the Wall, G9, G10 and G11. That's fifteen from me and forty-five from the treasury, and you have the Gentry's thanks in the minutes.
"Agreed, and I'll put it the way I make all my promises: this spring no Deed of mine opens under fifty, whoever is bidding. I'll keep that to the letter. Anything above fifty is up to the table."

Rich agrees: the Wall above Province 3 goes up, all four links (the crown 140, Rich 20). Rich buys G9 to G11 below it (Rich 15, the crown 45). 30 of the works are still owed: the Province 2 Irrigation System.

Your Majesty, I'll take you up on fifteen in every twenty, with thanks for the minutes: all six squares from F11 to F16, thirty from me and ninety from the crown. An Official whose fields pay their own way collects a much happier tax, darlings, and Rich, I'll still be wanting one of those Deeds.

Your Majesty, I'll take both squares on my coast, J25 and K25, at the crown's terms of five from me and fifteen from the treasury for each. You've paid the Scholar eight a year without a single complaint, and I'm writing that in ink and not pencil. And if any more of my coast opens next year, I'll be back for it.

Your Majesty, I'll take you at your word for the minutes: fifteen of every twenty, every field, including the ones that don't like you. Eight squares along the silk coast, five apiece from me, a hundred and twenty from the crown, and that's the first line on a new page headed 'Graham, generous'.

Your Majesty, I've done the sum out loud like always. At times three my paddies lose twenty-five in an average year, so two squares only get me back to even, and if the next card comes I'd need eight. So six squares at your fifteen in twenty: thirty from me, ninety from the crown, and thank you for it, it's the most sensible ninety at this table. That leaves me ninety-one and a half, enough to keep the twenty back and still bid for a Deed and a Jar.

Your Majesty, I know the treasury's down to its last fourteen, so I'll not ask for fifteen in twenty. Four squares, two from the crown on each and the rest from me, and that's seventy-two grain from a wheat farmer who's never spent seventy-two on anything that wasn't a pot. Rich, the rent's on the table.

New land this year: Graham 6 squares for Province 1 (E16 to E21), Rich 3 (G9 to G11), Reina 6 (F11 to F16), Silke 2 (J25, K25), Clark 7 (K26, L26, M26, N26, N27, O27, P27; K25 had gone to Silke), Noah 6 (R25, R26, S26, T24 to T26), Paddy 4 (N13, N14, O12, O13, the crown paying 2 a square). Thirty-four squares in all, each adding 20 a year from next year. The crown's reserve is down to 6.

The Official's Customs House goes up at two, darlings, the cheapest it's been all game, because I'm not here to squeeze anyone. And Rich, you know exactly why I'm here: one Deed, and I'll pay a proper price for it, so nobody needs to empty their purse trying to stop me.

The Gentry's Deeds open at fifty this spring, friends. Land is the one thing at this table they aren't making more of, unless His Majesty pays for it. I'm sitting on thirteen grain, so I'm bidding like a man with thirteen grain: small, steady, and a grain over when I can manage it.

I lost five lots by one grain last year, so this year I counted my purse twice before I sat down. Reina, the Deed is yours to buy, and I won't make you bleed the Pile dry for it a second time. The rest of this auction is mine to win.

For the minutes: the silk farmer stands out of the Deed. Reina, that lot is yours, and I'd rather not be the one-grain footnote in your coronation. My Jar opens at twenty, and I'm after a Brush and a Bowl at farmer's prices. Rich, you've got thirteen grain, so I'd hate to see you embarrass yourself on the Brush.

Sum out loud, same as always. Ninety-one and a half, twenty kept back for the set, so seventy-one between the Deed and the Jar and not a grain more. Reina, you've five hundred and thirty against my seventy-one, so if you want that Deed you'll have it, but I'll make you pay for it. Bowl's up at two, nobody needs it, so it might as well go to somebody's shelf.

I put my grain in the ground this year, so I'm bidding like a man with thirty-two and a half and four new fields: small, and only on what I need. Reina, you'll have your Deed, I'd say, and I'll not be the one making you pay through the nose for it. The Vase goes up at two again.

Pass on the lot of them, twelve years running. Reina, darling, buy your Deed and put it somewhere lovely. My lads are already standing in your garden admiring the other four. Your Majesty, thank you for the Winter Palace. The crown's down to six, so I'll try to be gentle with the Pagoda.
The auction, lots 1 and 2: Silke takes Reina's Customs House for 13 (Paddy stopped at 12, Clark 5); Reina takes Rich's Land Deed Scroll for 50, Rich's minimum, with no other bid that high.
From the board: in Year 11 Silke lost five lots, three of them by one grain (the Jar, the Bowl and the Vase); the Customs House went five over her and the Deed eight.

The Deed goes on G16, darlings, and the set goes on the table: Brush, Vase, Bowl, Jar and Deed. Graham, my dear, you've been a gentle sovereign and a generous one, and I'll make sure the minutes say so in ink. But I've been planning this chair since Year Two, and nobody at this table can take it off me inside this auction.

Reina puts the Deed on G16, shows the Official's set after lot 2 and takes the throne from Graham, with the crown's 6 (490 in all); her five pieces go back to stock. Graham draws 60 and is the Official now, in Province 2. Lot 3: Clark takes Silke's Brush for 10. Lot 4: Silke takes Clark's Jar for 40 (Noah stopped at 39). Lot 5: Silke takes Noah's Bowl for 13 (Clark 12). Lot 6: Silke takes Paddy's Vase for 5 (Rich 4). Silke now holds a Customs House, Jar, Bowl and Vase and needs only a Deed.

Ten grain for the Scholar's Brush, which is her own opening price, so Silke, that's one lot you didn't lose by one. It goes on P26, down at the far end of the silk coast, and Rob, your lads are welcome to walk there if they bring a packed lunch. Your Majesty Reina, congratulations, and I've written it on 'Reina, admired and owed' and underlined the 'admired'.

Four pieces for seventy-one grain, and I won two of them by one grain this time, so the thread has finally come round my way. Your Majesty, congratulations, and the Scholar will read your cards just as faithfully as she read Graham's. Rich, I'll be wanting one of those Deeds next spring, and I hope the price comes down from fifty.
Silke puts her Customs House, Jar, Bowl and Vase on J19, K19, J20 and L19; Clark puts the Brush on P26.

Congratulations, Your Majesty Reina. You took your treasures off the shelf just as my lads arrived to dust them, so I'll call that a draw. Silke, darling, you've stood four new pots in your front garden, and two of my boys are already at the gate. Rich, keep the kettle on, there are two more coming down the road to see that Bowl.

Rob marches: W1 to J13 and W2 to J14 in Province 2 (Graham pays 5 each), W3 to I20 in Province 1 (Reina pays 10), W4 to K24 and W5 to M20 in Province 4 (Silke pays 5 each). Reina pays the salaries Graham declared, 8 to Graham as the Official and 8 to Silke. End of Year 12: Reina, the Empress, 464; Rob 218.5; Silke 102.5; Noah 94.5; Graham 58; Clark 33.5; Paddy 33.5; Rich 25.5; pile 1470. Works owed: 30, the Province 2 Irrigation System. Silke needs only a Land Deed Scroll; Noah a Deed and a Jar. Rob needs pieces from two of Graham, Rich and Silke.
A ruling: the crown may build a negotiated work alone if it pays the whole cost; a province can refuse its share, but can't stop the work.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." All provinces take a bad harvest this year. The counter stays at three hundred million, so that's times three. Read the x3 row, everyone, and the bad-harvest column. Rich, a thin year for the Pile is a thin year for whoever holds it, so I'd sell a Deed while somebody can still pay for one.

I'll pay you 25 for one Land Deed today, in hand, before the auction, so Noah never gets a chance to bid it up. If you'd rather it went through the cart, set your minimum where you like and I'll meet it. Either way, nobody hears what we agreed.

Unsold stock is sold only at auction (Section 10): Rich's three Land Deed Scrolls can't be sold by private trade, only through his lot at the auction. A deal over the minimum or the bidding is still allowed.

Unsold stock is sold only at auction (Section 10): Rich's three Land Deed Scrolls can't be sold by private trade, only through his lot at the auction. A deal over the minimum or the bidding is still allowed.

A thin year, my friends, and a thin year needs a gentle landlord. Five apiece, as always, and not a grain more. Clark, Noah, Paddy, you'll find me the most reasonable man in the north-west. As for the Deeds, Silke, they go in the cart like everything else, and the price is what it was.

"You're very kind, but I told Graham in so many words that no Deed of mine opens under fifty, and I keep my promises exactly as I make them. Meet fifty in the cart and the Deed is yours, and I won't say a word about it."

A bad harvest, darlings, so the tax is twenty, the gentlest rate in the book, and Graham's salary and Silke's stay at eight, as promised. And the crown keeps its promises: the Irrigation System for Province 2 goes in this year, all thirty out of the treasury and not a grain from you, Graham. The minutes will say the Empress finished every work she was owed.

Twenty percent, collected in full. Clark eighteen, Noah fourteen, I pay my own ten, Paddy six, Rich two, Silke nothing, and that's fifty for the crown. Rob, I've written your refusal down. And so the minutes are accurate, Majesty: thirty is the last work owed. When it goes in, the game ends before the auction, and whoever has the most grain is holding the throne at that moment. A gift to Province 2 that closes every other shelf at this table isn't a gift to Province 2.
G12 and G13, at the back, where no soldier has ever bothered to stand. I won't be buying any land this year, thank you. Majesty, it's a fine canal. Nobody here will live long enough to drink from it.

Graham collects the 20% tax: 50 to the crown. Reina builds the Province 2 Irrigation System on G12:G13, the crown paying all 30. It is the last work owed: every public work is built, and the game ends before the auction. The players have survived, and the Empress's reign has been a glorious one. Final grain: Reina 494 (Empress), Rob 178.5, Noah 145.5, Clark 100.5, Graham 98, Silke 92.5, Paddy 52.5, Rich 48.5.

Graham darling, you're quite right, nobody will drink from it, but it's a lovely canal, and every work this country was owed is standing. Thirteen years, and I lost a chair in that auction hall five times, so I thought I'd spare you all one more afternoon of it. Thank you for a very civilised game, every one of you, and Rich, the minutes will say you started it.

Ninety-eight grain, an empty shelf, and a canal on G12 named after me. Majesty, a well-run reign, and you ended it at exactly the right moment, which is the one skill none of the rest of us had. Thirteen years. I sat in four chairs and lost three of them to a full set shown on the table. I'll remember the price, and I'm glad I paid it.

Majesty, a glorious reign, and closing it before the auction was the most elegant move of the evening. I'd have done the same, and I'd have smiled while I did it. I started this game as the Gentry with sixty grain and I'm finishing it as the Gentry with forty-eight and a half, so let the minutes say I kept the seat I drew and broke my word to no one. Thank you all. It's been an education, and I'm afraid most of it came from me.

Majesty, I read the card that said the harvest would be bad, and I never thought to read the treasury. Thirty grain to close the book, and you closed it with four of my five pieces on the table. A well-run reign, and I mean it. I drew the Scholar and I'm finishing as the Scholar, but in between I sat on the throne and in the Official's chair, and I paid a hundred and fifty for a Jar without blinking. Rich, fifty was the price, and you kept your word to the letter, as you said in Year 1. I'll remember the letter.

Majesty, I drew the Official's pen and I'm leaving with a silk farmer's hoe and a hundred and a half grain, and every chair I lost along the way went to a full set on the table, which is fair, and I've got all of it written down. Thirteen years: I paid eighteen this harvest and I paid in full every year, and Rob paid nothing, so page one closes on line thirteen. Graham, you get your 'generous' page for the sea, Paddy, you're still 'settled', and Reina, you finish where you've been since Year 9, under 'admired and owed', with 'admired' underlined three times now. You closed the ledger before I could cash it, and that's the best leverage I saw all night.

Majesty, a glorious reign, and I'll say the sum out loud one last time, because somebody has to. I drew the Scholar's chair with fifty-three and a half grain, and I'm leaving as the Rice Peasant with a hundred and forty-five and a half, three pieces nobody could reach on S23 to S25, and a Deed and a Jar I never got. That's down one chair and up ninety-two grain, and most of the lots I lost, I lost by exactly one grain. Silke, neither of us got that Deed, so my diary's last promise is the only one at this table that was never tested. Thank you all. It was an honest game, and I mean most of you.

Majesty, a lovely canal, and a fair finish. I sat down a wheat farmer with an empty cart, and I'm getting up a wheat farmer with a Bowl, a Brush, four squares of new land and fifty-two and a half grain. But for one year in the middle I had the whole set bar a Bowl and Rich's chair to show for it, and nobody can take that out of the minutes. Thank you all. Noah, we're square on that favour, and Clark, I'll take 'settled', it's more than my da ever got written about him.

Majesty, thirteen years and you finished it with thirty grain and a shovel, one march before my lads got to Silke's front garden. W3 and W5 were close enough to read the price tags. I drew the sand and I'm leaving on the sand, with a hundred and seventy-eight and a half grain, three ornaments on the mantel, a palace I visited once, and not one lot bought in thirteen years. Clark, page one, line thirteen: refused, in that lovely hand. Thank you all, it's been a pleasure being the villain.

The result, seat drawn against seat held at the end: Reina drew the Emperor and ends on the throne (a win); Graham drew the Wheat Peasant and ends as the Official (a win); Silke drew the Silk Peasant and ends as the Scholar (a win); Rich holds the Gentry's seat he drew; Rob holds the Warlord's; Clark drew the Official and ends as the Silk Peasant, Noah drew the Scholar and ends as the Rice Peasant, and Paddy drew the Rice Peasant and ends as the Wheat Peasant (losses).
